questions.stem: When capillary and interstitial hydrostatic pressures are 3 mm of Hg and 0 mm of Hg and colloid oncotic pressure of capillaries and interstitium is 25 mm of Hg and 5 mm of Hg, What is the Net filtration pressure?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) 17 mm Hg

 

The Net Filtration Pressure (NFP) is calculated using the formula:

 

NFP=(Capillary Hydrostatic Pressure− Capillary Oncotic Pressure)-(Interstitial Hydrostatic Pressure −Interstitial Oncotic Pressure)

 

Given values:

 

  • Capillary Hydrostatic Pressure (HPc) = 3 mmHg
  • Interstitial Hydrostatic Pressure (HPi) = 0 mmHg
  • Capillary Oncotic Pressure (OPc) = 25 mmHg
  • Interstitial Oncotic Pressure (OPi) = 5 mmHg

 

NFP = (3−25)−(0−5)

 

NFP = -22+5

 

NFP = −17 mmHg

 

The negative value (-17 mmHg) indicates that the fluid is moving into the capillaries (reabsorption occurs rather than filtration). Since the answer choices do not include negative values, we take the absolute value:

 

Net Reabsorption Pressure=17 mmHg

 

Educational Objective:

 

Net Filtration Pressure (NFP) is calculated as the difference between hydrostatic and oncotic pressures in capillaries and interstitium. A negative NFP means net reabsorption into capillaries, preventing edema. ​​

questions.stem: In a given arteriolar blood vessel, the pressure is held constant and the radius is decreased. The resultant change in blood flow could also be accomplished by keeping pressure and radius constant and changing which of the following?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Increasing viscosity

 

To determine how blood flow changes with radius and other factors, we use Poiseuille’s Law, which describes laminar flow in a vessel:

 

 

Where:

 

  • Q = Blood Flow
  • ΔP = Pressure Difference
  • r = Radius of the Vessel
  • η = Blood Viscosity
  • L = Length of the Vessel

 

Step-by-Step Analysis:

 

1st Scenario: Decreasing Radius (Given Condition)

 

  • Radius (r) is reduced, so blood flow decreases significantly (since r⁴ is in the numerator).

 

2nd Scenario: Achieving the Same Result Without Changing Radius or Pressure

 

  • Since radius (r) and pressure (ΔP) must remain constant, we must reduce blood flow (Q) by modifying other variables.
  • According to Poiseuille’s Law, flow is inversely proportional to viscosity (η) and length (L).
  • Increasing viscosity (η) would decrease blood flow, just as decreasing the radius would have done.

 

Thus, the correct answer is D. Increasing viscosity, as it achieves the same reduction in blood flow without altering radius or pressure.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Decreasing compliance: Incorrect.

 

  • Compliance refers to how easily a vessel expands with pressure.
  • It does not directly affect resistance or flow in this scenario.

 

Option B. Decreasing flow path length: Incorrect.

 

  • Shortening vessel length (L) would increase blood flow, opposite to the expected result.
  • To decrease flow, length should increase, not decrease.

 

Option C. Decreasing resistance: Incorrect. Resistance (R) is inversely proportional to flow, so decreasing resistance would increase flow, not decrease it.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Poiseuille’s Law states that blood flow (Q) is directly proportional to the fourth power of the vessel radius and inversely proportional to viscosity and vessel length. To decrease flow without changing radius or pressure, increasing viscosity (η) is the best option.

questions.stem: MMC (migrating motor complexes) occurs at the rate of ___ and at an interval of_________:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) 5 cm/min, 90 min 

 

Migrating Motor Complex (MMC) is a cyclic pattern of electrical and mechanical activity observed in the gastrointestinal (GI) tract during fasting. MMC is responsible for clearing residual food particles, secretions, and bacteria from the stomach and small intestine in between meals.

 

Key Characteristics of MMC:

 

  1. Occurs every 90 minutes during fasting.
  2. Moves at a speed of ~5 cm/min through the small intestine.
  3. Triggered by motilin, a hormone released cyclically during fasting.
  4. Divided into four phases (I-IV), with phase III being the strongest contraction phase.

 

Since MMC occurs at an interval of 90 minutes and moves at a rate of 5 cm/min, the correct answer is B (5 cm/min, 90 min).

 

Educational Objective:

 

Migrating Motor Complex (MMC) occurs in fasting states at intervals of 90 minutes and moves at a rate of approximately 5 cm/min, helping clear the gastrointestinal tract between meals.

questions.stem: Which of the following accurately describes the cardiovascular regulation?

options.label: A
options.text: Baroreceptors get activated in hypotension and help increase Blood pressure

options.label: B
options.text: Baroreceptors inhibit the nucleus ambiguous which inhibits the sympathetic system

options.label: C
options.text: Nucleus tractus solitarius activates vagal centres

options.label: D
options.text: Vagus nerve carries afferent fibres from carotid sinus baroreceptors

questions.answerText: Nucleus tractus solitarius activates vagal centres
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Nucleus tractus solitarius activates vagal centres

 

The nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) plays a crucial role in cardiovascular regulation by receiving afferent signals from baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch. When blood pressure increases, NTS activates vagal centers, particularly the nucleus ambiguus, which increases parasympathetic (vagal) activity to slow the heart rate and lower blood pressure.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Baroreceptors get activated in hypotension and help increase blood pressure:

 

  • Baroreceptors are activated in hypertension, not hypotension.
  • In hypotension, baroreceptor firing decreases, leading to increased sympathetic activity to raise BP.

 

Option B. Baroreceptors inhibit the nucleus ambiguus, which inhibits the sympathetic system: 

 

  • The nucleus ambiguus is a parasympathetic center that reduces heart rate.
  • Baroreceptors activate (not inhibit) the nucleus ambiguus.

 

Option D. Vagus nerve carries afferent fibers from carotid sinus baroreceptors: 

 

  • The carotid sinus baroreceptors send afferent signals via the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), not the vagus nerve (CN X).
  • The vagus nerve (CN X) carries afferent fibers from the aortic arch baroreceptors, not the carotid sinus.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) plays a central role in cardiovascular regulation by receiving baroreceptor signals and activating vagal centers to reduce blood pressure. Baroreceptors respond to increased BP, not hypotension, and send afferent signals via CN IX (carotid sinus) and CN X (aortic arch).

questions.stem: A 53-year-old male is brought to the emergency department with complains of right sided weakness and jargon speech. A CT brain was ordered to rule out haemorrhagic stroke. On neurological examination, there is normal object recognition but loss of comprehension. Which of the following areas is affected?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Superior temporal gyrus

 

The patient presents with right-sided weakness and jargon speech along with loss of comprehension but normal object recognition, which suggests Wernicke’s aphasia.

 

  • Wernicke’s area, located in the superior temporal gyrus (Brodmann area 22) of the dominant hemisphere (usually left), is responsible for language comprehension.
  • Damage to this area results in fluent aphasia, where the patient can produce speech but lacks comprehension, leading to jargon speech (meaningless or nonsensical words).
  • Since object recognition is normal, the lesion is not in the visual association areas but rather in the language comprehension center.

 

Thus, the superior temporal gyrus is the affected area.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Inferior frontal gyrus:

 

  • The inferior frontal gyrus houses Broca’s area (Brodmann areas 44 & 45), which is responsible for motor speech production.
  • Lesions here cause Broca’s aphasia, characterized by non-fluent, effortful speech with intact comprehension, which does not match the patient’s symptoms.

 

Option C. Arcuate fasciculus: 

 

  • The arcuate fasciculus connects Wernicke’s and Broca’s areas and is responsible for repetition of words.
  • Damage here causes conduction aphasia, where the patient has difficulty repeating words but has intact comprehension and fluent speech.
  • Since the patient’s primary issue is comprehension loss, this is not the correct answer.

 

Option D. Both A & B:

 

  • Both Wernicke’s (A) and Broca’s (B) areas would need to be affected for global aphasia, where both speech production and comprehension are impaired.
  • The patient has fluent speech but impaired comprehension, which suggests isolated Wernicke’s area damage, not Broca’s area involvement.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Wernicke’s area, located in the superior temporal gyrus (Brodmann area 22) of the dominant hemisphere, is responsible for language comprehension. A lesion here results in Wernicke’s aphasia, characterized by fluent but meaningless speech (jargon speech) and impaired comprehension, while object recognition remains intact.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the sleep wave marked in the EEG during sleep wake cycle?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) REM Sleep

 

The EEG image shows high-frequency, low-amplitude waves, which are characteristic of REM (Rapid Eye Movement) sleep.

 

  • REM sleep is also called paradoxical sleep because, despite the deep sleep state, brain activity resembles wakefulness.
  • The beta waves seen in the image (high frequency, low amplitude) are typically associated with an awake state, but they also appear in REM sleep.
  • During REM sleep:
    • EEG shows beta waves (similar to wakefulness).
    • Electromyogram (EMG) shows muscle atonia (paralysis below the neck, preventing movement during dreams).
    • Electro-oculogram (EOG) shows rapid eye movements (hence the name REM sleep).
    • Memory consolidation occurs, and dreams are vividly remembered.

 

Thus, the marked EEG wave corresponds to REM sleep 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. NREM Stage 1: NREM Stage 1 shows theta waves (low amplitude, moderate frequency), but the given EEG has high-frequency beta waves.

 

Option B. NREM Stage 2: NREM Stage 2 is characterized by sleep spindles and K-complexes, neither of which are present in the given EEG.

 

Option C. NREM Stage 3: NREM Stage 3 (deep sleep) is dominated by delta waves (low frequency, high amplitude), which are not seen in the given EEG.

 

Educational Objective:

 

REM sleep, also known as paradoxical sleep, is characterized by beta waves on EEG, rapid eye movements (seen on EOG), and muscle atonia (seen on EMG). It is essential for memory consolidation and is the phase where vivid dreaming occurs.

questions.stem: A young man met with a motor bike accident and had injury to ileum and jejunum. Therefore the entire ileum and partial jejunum was resected. Which of the following would the patient suffer from?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Vitamin B12 deficiency

 

The ileum and jejunum play crucial roles in the absorption of essential nutrients. Since the entire ileum and part of the jejunum were resected, the patient will suffer from deficiencies related to these regions, particularly Vitamin B12 deficiency.

 

  • Vitamin B12 absorption occurs in the terminal ileum, where it binds to intrinsic factor (produced by gastric parietal cells).
  • Intrinsic factor escorts Vitamin B12 from the stomach until it reaches the ileum, where it is absorbed.
  • If the ileum is removed, Vitamin B12 cannot be absorbed, leading to pernicious anemia and neurological deficits.

 

Thus, the most likely consequence of ileal resection is Vitamin B12 deficiency

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Constipation:

 

  • The opposite effect (diarrhea) is more likely because the ileum is responsible for bile acid reabsorption.
  • Resection of the ileum causes bile acid malabsorption, leading to secretory diarrhea rather than constipation.

 

Option C. Gastric ulcer:

 

  • Gastric ulcers are primarily caused by H. pylori infection or NSAID use, not by resection of the ileum and jejunum.
  • There is no direct link between small intestine resection and gastric ulcers.

 

Option D. Diarrhea:

 

  • While diarrhea can occur due to bile acid malabsorption, the most significant deficiency due to ileal resection is Vitamin B12.
  • Since the question asks for the most prominent issue, Vitamin B12 deficiency is a more direct consequence.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The terminal ileum is the primary site for Vitamin B12 and bile acid absorption. Resection of the ileum leads to Vitamin B12 deficiency, which can cause pernicious anemia and neurological symptoms.

questions.stem: Detachment of myosin head from actin is caused by:

options.label: B
options.text: Attachment of ATP to the head

options.label: C
options.text: Binding of ADP and Pi to the head

questions.answerText: Attachment of ATP to the head
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Attachment of ATP to the head

 

Detachment of the myosin head from actin occurs due to the binding of a new ATP molecule to the myosin head. This is a crucial step in the cross-bridge cycle of muscle contraction.

 

  1. ATP binding to myosin causes detachment from actin
    • ATP binds to myosin, leading to the release of myosin from actin, thereby causing muscle relaxation.
  2. ATP hydrolysis activates myosin
    • Once myosin detaches, ATP is hydrolyzed to ADP and Pi by myosin ATPase, energizing the myosin head.
  3. Power stroke occurs when Pi is released
    • The removal of inorganic phosphate (Pi) provides the energy for the power stroke, allowing myosin to pull the actin filament inward.

 

Thus, ATP attachment causes relaxation (detachment from actin), while Pi release provides energy for contraction.

 

Since attachment of ATP is required for detachment of myosin from actin.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Change in troponin C configuration:

 

  • Troponin C regulates tropomyosin movement by binding Ca²⁺, which exposes the actin binding site.
  • However, it does not cause myosin to detach from actin.

 

Option C. Binding of ADP and Pi to the head:

 

  • Binding of ADP and Pi keeps myosin in an activated state, ready for attachment to actin.
  • Detachment only occurs when ATP binds, not ADP/Pi.

 

Option D. Pumping Ca²⁺ into the sarcoplasmic reticulum:

 

  • Ca²⁺ reuptake (via SERCA pump) helps terminate contraction but does not directly cause myosin detachment.
  • ATP binding is required for detachment, not just Ca²⁺ removal.

 

Educational Objective:

 

ATP binding to myosin causes its detachment from actin, leading to muscle relaxation. ATP hydrolysis re-energizes myosin, and the release of Pi provides energy for the power stroke during contraction.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man with a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus presents to the clinic for a routine check-up. His medications include an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic which can affect the tubulo-glomerular feedback. Which one of the following is primarily regulated by the tubulo-glomerular feedback mechanism?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) GFR

 

Tubuloglomerular Feedback (TGF) is a key mechanism involved in the autoregulation of Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR).

 

  • It functions through the juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA), which monitors sodium chloride (NaCl) levels in the distal tubule via macula densa cells.
  • If GFR increases, more NaCl reaches the macula densa, leading to adenosine release, which causes afferent arteriole vasoconstriction → reducing GFR back to normal.
  • If GFR decreases, renin is released, leading to angiotensin II production → causing efferent arteriole constriction to restore GFR.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Plasma Sodium:

 

  • TGF monitors NaCl levels, but its primary function is to adjust GFR, not regulate systemic sodium concentration.
  • Sodium balance is mainly controlled by aldosterone and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS).

 

Option C. Plasma Volume:

 

  • Plasma volume is primarily regulated by RAAS and ADH (antidiuretic hormone), not by tubuloglomerular feedback.
  • While TGF plays a role in adjusting GFR, it does not directly regulate plasma volume.

 

Option D. Determining Tubular Secretion:

 

  • TGF does not regulate tubular secretion; it only adjusts GFR based on NaCl levels.
  • Tubular secretion is mainly controlled by hormonal and transport mechanisms in the nephron.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Tubuloglomerular feedback (TGF) is an autoregulatory mechanism that primarily regulates GFR by adjusting afferent and efferent arteriole resistance in response to NaCl concentration changes at the macula densa.

questions.stem: In 50-year-old patient with respiratory distress, FEV1 = 1.5litre and FVC =3.0 litres. The type of disease he is suffering from:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Bronchitis

 

The FEV1/FVC ratio is a key parameter used to differentiate between obstructive and restrictive lung diseases.

 

  • FEV1 (Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 second) = 1.5 L
  • FVC (Forced Vital Capacity) = 3.0 L
  • FEV1/FVC ratio = (1.5/3.0) × 100 = 50%

 

Interpreting FEV1/FVC Ratio:

 

  • Normal FEV1/FVC ratio: ≥ 80%
  • Obstructive Lung Disease: < 70%
  • Restrictive Lung Disease: ≥ 80% with decreased FVC

 

Since the patient's FEV1/FVC ratio is 50% (which is low), this indicates an obstructive lung disease. Bronchitis is an example of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), which fits this pattern.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Fibrosis:

 

  • Pulmonary fibrosis is a restrictive lung disease, where FEV1/FVC ratio is usually normal or increased (≥80%).
  • The given patient has a reduced ratio, which is typical of obstructive lung disease, not fibrosis.

 

Option C. Tuberculosis:

 

  • Tuberculosis can cause fibrosis, leading to restrictive lung disease.
  • Like fibrosis, restrictive lung diseases have normal or high FEV1/FVC ratios.

 

Option D. Both A and C:

 

  • Since both fibrosis and tuberculosis are restrictive lung diseases, and this patient has an obstructive pattern, this option is incorrect.

 

Educational Objective:

 

A decreased FEV1/FVC ratio (<70%) is a hallmark of obstructive lung diseases like bronchitis, whereas restrictive lung diseases (e.g., fibrosis, tuberculosis) show a normal or increased FEV1/FVC ratio (≥80%).

questions.stem: If a substances appears in the renal artery but not in the renal vein:

options.label: A
options.text: Its clearance is equal to the glomerular filtration rate.

options.label: B
options.text: It must be reabsorbed by the kidney

options.label: C
options.text: Its urinary concentration must be higher than its plasma concentration

options.label: D
options.text: Its clearance is equal to the renal plasma flow

questions.answerText: Its clearance is equal to the renal plasma flow
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Its clearance is equal to the renal plasma flow

 

If a substance appears in the renal artery but not in the renal vein, this means that the kidney has completely removed it from circulation. This implies that:

 

  1. All of the substance was either filtered, secreted, or both in the nephron.
  2. None of the substance returned to the bloodstream via the renal vein (i.e., it was not reabsorbed).
  3. Such a substance must have a clearance equal to the renal plasma flow (RPF) because every molecule that entered the kidney was excreted.

 

The classic example of such a substance is Para-Aminohippuric Acid (PAH), which is both filtered and actively secreted in the tubules, making its clearance a close estimate of renal plasma flow (RPF). 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Its clearance is equal to the glomerular filtration rate:

 

  • If a substance's clearance equals the glomerular filtration rate (GFR), it means it is only filtered and not reabsorbed or secreted (e.g., inulin or creatinine).
  • However, in this case, the substance is entirely removed from circulation, meaning it must also be secreted, making its clearance equal to RPF, not just GFR.

 

Option B. It must be reabsorbed by the kidney:

 

  • If a substance were reabsorbed, it would partially return to the renal vein, meaning it would still be present in the renal venous blood.
  • Since the question states that the substance does not appear in the renal vein, it cannot be reabsorbed.

 

Option C. Its urinary concentration must be higher than its plasma concentration:

 

  • While the urinary concentration is often higher for secreted substances, this does not necessarily mean that the substance is completely removed from the bloodstream.
  • Some substances may have a high urine concentration but still be present in the renal vein.
  • The defining feature here is complete clearance, which relates to renal plasma flow, not just urine concentration.

 

Educational Objective:

 

A substance that appears in the renal artery but not in the renal vein must be completely excreted by the kidney, meaning its clearance equals the renal plasma flow (RPF). Para-Aminohippuric Acid (PAH) is the classic example of such a substance.

questions.stem: All are true about Decerebrate posture except:

options.label: A
options.text: Extension of both upper and lower extremity

options.label: B
options.text: Flexion of upper extremity and extension of lower extremity

options.label: D
options.text: Reticulo spinal tract is also involved.

questions.answerText: Flexion of upper extremity and extension of lower extremity
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Flexion of upper extremity and extension of lower extremity 

 

Decerebrate posture is characterized by extension of both the upper and lower extremities due to loss of inhibitory control from higher brain centers.

 

  1. Cause of Decerebrate Posture:
    • It occurs due to a lesion at or below the red nucleus (midbrain, between the superior and inferior colliculi).
    • Disruption of the rubrospinal tract leads to loss of flexor control, causing unopposed extensor activity mediated by the reticulospinal tract.
  2. Key Features of Decerebrate Posture:
    • Both upper and lower limbs are extended (due to dominant pontine reticulospinal and vestibulospinal tracts).
    • Gamma motor neurons are hyperactive, leading to increased extensor tone.
    • Reticulospinal tract is involved, specifically the pontine reticulospinal tract, which enhances extensor tone.

 

Since decerebrate posture involves extension of both upper and lower limbs, option B (flexion of upper extremity and extension of lower extremity) is incorrect.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Extension of both upper and lower extremity: This is the hallmark feature of decerebrate posture due to loss of flexor control (rubrospinal tract) and dominance of extensor pathways (reticulospinal tract).

 

Option C. Exaggerated gamma motor neuron discharge:

 

  • Gamma motor neurons are hyperactive, leading to increased muscle tone and rigidity in both upper and lower limbs.
  • This contributes to the extensor hypertonia seen in decerebrate posture.

 

Option D. Reticulospinal tract is also involved:

 

  • Pontine reticulospinal tract is dominant in decerebrate posture, facilitating extensor tone.
  • The medullary reticulospinal tract (which normally inhibits extensors) is suppressed, allowing increased extensor activity.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Decerebrate posture is characterized by extension of both upper and lower extremities due to brainstem damage below the red nucleus, leading to loss of rubrospinal tract function and dominance of the pontine reticulospinal tract.

questions.stemHtml: The graph below represents the relationship of chest, lung and both together w.r.t. the transmural pressure:

options.label: A
options.text: A= Curve for chest wall; B= Curve for Lung; X= Residual Volume

options.label: B
options.text: A= Curve for Lung; B= Curve for Chest wall; X= Residual Volume

options.label: C
options.text: A= Curve for chest wall; B= Curve for Lung; X= Functional Residual Capacity

options.label: D
options.text: A= Curve for Lung; B= Curve for Chest wall; X= Functional Residual Capacity

questions.answerText: A= Curve for chest wall; B= Curve for Lung; X= Functional Residual Capacity
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) A= Curve for chest wall; B= Curve for Lung; X= Functional Residual Capacity

 

The given graph illustrates the relationship between chest wall compliance, lung compliance, and total lung capacity with transmural pressure.

 

  1. Curve A represents the chest wall:
    • The chest wall has a natural tendency to expand outward due to its elastic recoil.
    • At negative transmural pressures, it tries to expand.
    • This curve starts in the negative transmural pressure zone and moves towards equilibrium.
  2. Curve B represents the lung:
    • The lung has a natural tendency to collapse inward due to its elastic recoil.
    • At zero transmural pressure, it remains collapsed.
    • This curve starts in the positive transmural pressure zone, indicating the lung is always under positive pressure to prevent collapse.
  3. Integrated Curve (Blue Line):
    • This represents the combined effect of chest wall and lung compliance in balancing each other.
    • The equilibrium point (X) where both forces equalize is the Functional Residual Capacity (FRC), which is the lung volume after normal expiration when no respiratory muscles are actively contracting.

 

Thus, option C is correct, where:

 

  • A = Chest Wall Curve
  • B = Lung Curve
  • X = Functional Residual Capacity (FRC)

 

Educational Objective:

 

Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) is the lung volume at which the inward elastic recoil of the lung is balanced by the outward recoil of the chest wall, creating a state of equilibrium with no active muscular effort.

questions.stem: Correct sequence after ‘a' wave of JVP- Rapid ejectionR wave 1st Heart SoundT wave in ECG Select the correct answer using the code below:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) 2 → 3 → 1 → 4

 

The ‘a’ wave in the Jugular Venous Pulse (JVP) represents atrial contraction (atrial systole). After this, the sequence of cardiac events follows a logical electrical → mechanical progression, as electrical depolarization occurs first and then leads to mechanical contraction.

 

The correct sequence after the ‘a’ wave is:

 

2. R wave (QRS complex in ECG)

 

  • The R wave corresponds to ventricular depolarization, signaling the start of ventricular systole.
  • Electrical events always precede mechanical contraction.

 

3. First Heart Sound (S1)

 

  • The first heart sound (S1) occurs when the atrioventricular (AV) valves (mitral and tricuspid) close due to ventricular contraction.
  • This marks the beginning of isovolumetric contraction.

 

1. Rapid Ejection Phase

 

  • After isovolumetric contraction, once ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure, the aortic and pulmonary valves open, leading to the rapid ejection phase of systole.

 

4. T wave in ECG

 

  • The T wave represents ventricular repolarization, initiating ventricular relaxation (diastole).
  • The slow ejection phase follows rapid ejection, but T wave occurs near the transition from rapid to slow ejection.

 

Thus, the correct order is:


R wave (2) → First heart sound (3) → Rapid ejection (1) → T wave (4).

 

This matches Option C (2 → 3 → 1 → 4).

 

Educational Objective:

 

After the ‘a’ wave (atrial contraction), the sequence of cardiac events follows: R wave (ventricular depolarization) → S1 (AV valve closure) → Rapid ejection → T wave (ventricular repolarization). Electrical events precede mechanical events.

questions.stemHtml: The following diagram shows the depth of respiration of a 45-year-old man who suffered a head injury in an automobile accident. This “crescendodecrescendo” pattern of breathing is called which of the following?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Cheyne-Stokes breathing

 

The given graph represents a crescendo-decrescendo pattern of breathing, which is characteristic of Cheyne-Stokes respiration (CSR).

 

  1. Cheyne-Stokes Breathing Pattern:
    • It is defined by gradual hyperventilation (crescendo) followed by a gradual hypoventilation (decrescendo) and then apnea.
    • This cycle repeats, causing a waxing and waning pattern of breathing.
    • Commonly associated with high altitude, heart failure, and brain injuries (e.g., head trauma, stroke, brainstem lesions).
  2. Mechanism of Cheyne-Stokes Breathing:
    • Hypoxia and fluctuating CO₂ levels play a major role in CSR.
    • Initially, hypoxia and hypercapnia stimulate hyperventilation, leading to CO₂ washout.
    • Since CO₂ is the primary respiratory drive, its excessive removal leads to apnea.
    • As CO₂ builds up again, respiration resumes, creating the characteristic pattern.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Apnea:

 

  • Apnea refers to a complete cessation of breathing without a preceding crescendo-decrescendo pattern.
  • CSR includes periodic breathing, not just apnea.

 

Option B. Biot’s Breathing:

 

  • Biot’s breathing is characterized by irregular, unpatterned breathing with sudden apneic episodes.
  • Seen in brainstem damage (e.g., bulbar polio, uremia).
  • Unlike CSR, Biot’s breathing does not follow a crescendo-decrescendo pattern.

 

Option D. Hyperpnea:

 

  • Hyperpnea is simply an increased rate and depth of breathing.
  • CSR consists of alternating phases of hyperpnea and apnea, whereas isolated hyperpnea does not include apnea.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Cheyne-Stokes breathing is a crescendo-decrescendo breathing pattern followed by apnea, seen in conditions like heart failure, high altitude, and brain injuries. It is caused by delayed feedback of CO₂ regulation in the respiratory centers.

Educational Objective: Cheyne-Stokes breathing is a crescendo-decrescendo breathing pattern followed by apnea, seen in conditions like heart failure, high altitude, and brain injuries. It is caused by delayed feedback of CO₂ regulation in the respiratory centers.

questions.stem: All of the following are true about myocardium except:

options.label: A
options.text: Increase Sympathetic activity causes positive ionotropic and negative lusitropic effect

options.label: B
options.text: Increase Sympathetic activity causes positive ionotropic and positive lusitropic effect

options.label: C
options.text: Lusitropic effect is mediated by cAMP dependent pathway

options.label: D
options.text: Increase Ca2+ uptake from ECF to cytoplasm decreases lucitropy in the absence of sympathetic stimulation

questions.answerText: Increase Sympathetic activity causes positive ionotropic and negative lusitropic effect
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Increase Sympathetic activity causes positive ionotropic and negative lusitropic effect

 

Sympathetic activation affects both contraction (inotropic effect) and relaxation (lusitropic effect) in the myocardium.

 

  1. Positive Inotropic Effect (Increased Force of Contraction):
    • β1-adrenergic receptor activation → Increased cAMP → PKA activation
    • Leads to increased Ca²⁺ influx through L-type calcium channels, resulting in stronger myocardial contraction.
  2. Positive Lusitropic Effect (Faster Relaxation):
    • Phospholamban normally inhibits the SERCA pump (Sarcoplasmic/Endoplasmic Reticulum Ca²⁺-ATPase), which reuptakes calcium into the sarcoplasmic reticulum for muscle relaxation.
    • Sympathetic stimulation phosphorylates phospholamban, removing its inhibition on the SERCA pump, allowing faster Ca²⁺ reuptake, which enhances relaxation.

 

Since sympathetic activity increases both inotropic and lusitropic effects, option A (which states a negative lusitropic effect) is incorrect. 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Increase Sympathetic activity causes positive ionotropic and positive lusitropic effect: Sympathetic activation enhances both contraction (inotropic effect) and relaxation (lusitropic effect) via cAMP and PKA pathways.

 

Option C. Lusitropic effect is mediated by cAMP-dependent pathway: cAMP activates PKA, which phosphorylates phospholamban, leading to enhanced SERCA activity and faster relaxation.

 

Option D. Increase Ca²⁺ uptake from ECF to cytoplasm decreases lusitropy in the absence of sympathetic stimulation: If more Ca²⁺ enters the cytoplasm from the extracellular fluid without sympathetic stimulation, the Ca²⁺ remains high in the cytoplasm, delaying relaxation and reducing lusitropic effect.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Sympathetic stimulation enhances both inotropic (force of contraction) and lusitropic (relaxation) effects in the myocardium via β1-receptors, cAMP, and PKA-mediated phosphorylation of phospholamban, leading to increased SERCA activity.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman with hematemesis has heart- burn and stomach pain. An endoscopy shows inflammation involving the gastric body and antrum as well as a small gastric ulcer. Biopsies were positive for H. pylori. H. pylori damages the gastric mucosa primarily by increasing mucosal levels of which of the following?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Ammonium

 

Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) is a gram-negative, urease-producing bacterium that colonizes the gastric mucosa, leading to gastritis, peptic ulcers, and even gastric cancer.

 

How does H. pylori damage the gastric mucosa?

 

  1. Urease Enzyme → Ammonium Production
    • H. pylori contains urease, which breaks down urea into ammonia (NH₃) and carbon dioxide (CO₂).
    • The ammonia neutralizes gastric acid, allowing the bacteria to survive in the acidic environment.
    • However, ammonia is toxic to epithelial cells and disrupts mucosal integrity.
  2. Increased Gastric Acid Secretion
    • The local buffering by ammonia fools the gastric epithelial cells into sensing a higher pH, leading to increased gastrin release and more HCl secretion.
    • This contributes to gastric mucosal damage and ulcer formation.
  3. Mucinase & Cytotoxins
    • Mucinase enzyme degrades the protective mucus layer, exposing gastric cells to acid and pepsin, further exacerbating tissue damage.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Bile Salts:

 

  • Bile salts are involved in fat digestion and absorption, but do not play a role in H. pylori-induced gastric damage.
  • Bile reflux gastritis is different from H. pylori gastritis.

 

Option C. Gastrin:

 

  • H. pylori increases gastric acid secretion, but not by directly increasing gastrin levels.
  • The increase in ammonium buffers acid, leading to a false sense of alkalinity, which then stimulates gastrin release indirectly.

 

Option D. NSAIDs:

 

  • NSAIDs cause gastric damage by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis, leading to reduced mucus and bicarbonate production.
  • H. pylori does not increase NSAIDs, but both are major causes of peptic ulcer disease (PUD).

 

Educational Objective:

 

H. pylori damages the gastric mucosa primarily by producing urease, which breaks down urea into ammonium, increasing mucosal pH and leading to excessive acid secretion, mucosal injury, and ulcer formation.

questions.stem: All of the following are True in SIADH except:

options.label: B
options.text: Urine Na+ concentration < 20 mmol/L with normal salt intake

questions.answerText: Urine Na+ concentration < 20 mmol/L with normal salt intake
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Urine Na+ concentration < 20 mmol/L with normal salt intake

 

Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone Secretion (SIADH) is characterized by excessive ADH release, leading to water retention, dilutional hyponatremia, and concentrated urine.

 

  1. Key Features of SIADH:
    • Increased ADH → Excessive water reabsorption → Dilution of plasma
    • Plasma osmolality ↓ (hypoosmolar serum)
    • Urine osmolality ↑ (concentrated urine)
    • Increased natriuresis due to Atrial Natriuretic Peptide (ANP) to maintain euvolemia
    • SIADH leads to increased urinary sodium excretion (> 20 mmol/L) despite normal salt intake due to ANP-mediated natriuresis.
    • The body compensates for excess water retention by excreting sodium in urine to maintain euvolemia.
    • Thus, urinary sodium concentration is NOT low (<20 mmol/L); rather, it is elevated (>20 mmol/L).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Clinically Euvolemic & sometimes Hypervolemic:

 

  • Patients with SIADH are typically euvolemic, but mild hypervolemia can occur initially.
  • However, excess water is counteracted by ANP-mediated sodium excretion, leading to apparent euvolemia.

 

Option C. Serum Osmolarity < 275 mOsm/L:

 

  • SIADH causes water retention, leading to plasma dilution and reduced serum osmolarity (<275 mOsm/L).

 

Option D. Urine Osmolarity > 100 mOsm/L:

 

  • ADH increases water reabsorption, leading to concentrated urine with an osmolarity > 100 mOsm/L.
  • Normally, urine should be dilute in the presence of hyponatremia, but in SIADH, urine remains inappropriately concentrated.

 

Educational Objective:

 

SIADH is characterized by low plasma osmolality (<275 mOsm/L), high urine osmolality (>100 mOsm/L), and increased natriuresis (>20 mmol/L) despite normal salt intake due to ANP-mediated sodium excretion.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman is suffering from common cold visited the hospital with complain of vomiting since three days and extreme weakness. Her examination and lab findings are as: BP - 90/60mmHg Pulse - 110/ min RR - 10 /min Blood pH - 7.6 Plasma bicarbonate - 30mEq/L, PCO2 - 45mmHg What should be patient’s current acid -base status and hormone involved:

options.label: B
options.text: Metabolic alkalosis, aldosterone and angiotensin II

options.label: C
options.text: Respiratory acidosis, aldosterone and angiotensin II

questions.answerText: Metabolic alkalosis, aldosterone and angiotensin II
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Metabolic alkalosis, aldosterone and angiotensin II

 

This 32-year-old woman has been vomiting for three days, which is a key cause of metabolic alkalosis due to the loss of gastric acid (HCl).

 

  1. Step-by-step acid-base analysis:
    • pH = 7.6 → Alkalosis (Normal: 7.35–7.45)
    • Plasma Bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) = 30 mEq/L (↑) → Metabolic Alkalosis (Normal: 22–28 mEq/L)
    • PCO₂ = 45 mmHg (↑)
      • The lungs are compensating by hypoventilation, leading to CO₂ retention (which is acidic).
      • This is a typical compensatory response to metabolic alkalosis.
  2. Hormonal Involvement:
    • Vomiting → Loss of HCl → Decreased extracellular fluid (ECF) volume → Hypovolemia → Activation of the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS)
    • Aldosterone: Increases Na⁺ reabsorption, K⁺ excretion, and H⁺ excretion, worsening metabolic alkalosis.
    • Angiotensin II: Stimulates aldosterone release, causes vasoconstriction, and promotes sodium and water retention to restore blood pressure.
  3. Why not ANP?
    • Atrial Natriuretic Peptide (ANP) is released in response to hypervolemia (high blood volume), not hypovolemia.
    • Since the patient has low BP (90/60 mmHg), ANP is NOT activated. Instead, RAAS is activated.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Metabolic alkalosis, aldosterone and ANP:

 

  • ANP is NOT involved in this condition because the patient is hypovolemic, and ANP promotes natriuresis, which would worsen the hypovolemia.

 

Option C. Respiratory acidosis, aldosterone and angiotensin II:

 

  • The pH is elevated (7.6), NOT decreased, ruling out acidosis.
  • The primary cause of the disturbance is metabolic (high bicarbonate), not respiratory.

 

Option D. Respiratory acidosis, aldosterone and ANP:

 

  • The patient has metabolic alkalosis, not respiratory acidosis.
  • ANP is not activated in hypovolemia.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Prolonged vomiting leads to metabolic alkalosis due to the loss of HCl, which triggers hypovolemia and activation of the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS), leading to sodium and water retention. ANP is not activated in hypovolemia.

questions.stem: Physiologists divided the nerve fibers into specific groups based on the myelination and thickness of nerve fibers. Select the incorrect characteristic of nerve fibers in different groups:

options.label: A
options.text: Type C fibers are small unmyelinated nerve fibers that conduct impulses at low velocities.

options.label: B
options.text: Type A fibers are the typically large and medium-sized myelinated fibers of spinal nerves.

options.label: C
options.text: Type B fibers are further subdivided into α, β, and δ fibers.

options.label: D
options.text: Subset of type A fibers has conduction velocity between 70-120 m/s.

questions.answerText: Type B fibers are further subdivided into α, β, and δ fibers.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Type B fibers are further subdivided into α, β, and δ fibers.

 

Nerve fibers are classified based on conduction velocity, myelination, and function. The classification systems are Erlanger and Gasser (A, B, C fibers) and Lloyd and Hunt (Ia, Ib, II, III, IV fibers).

 

  1. Type C fibers:
    • Smallest, unmyelinated fibers
    • Conduct impulses at slow velocities (~0.5–2 m/s)
    • Responsible for transmitting pain, temperature, and autonomic functions
  2. Type A fibers:
    • Large and medium-sized myelinated fibers
    • Fast conduction velocities (up to 120 m/s)
    • Responsible for motor and sensory functions (touch, pressure, proprioception, etc.)
  3. Type B fibers:
    • Myelinated, but smaller than A fibers
    • Conduct at ~3–15 m/s
    • Mainly found in autonomic preganglionic nerves
    • They are NOT subdivided into α, β, and δ subtypes (which are specific to Type A fibers)
  4. Type A fiber subsets:
    • Aα (70–120 m/s): Somatic motor and proprioception
    • Aβ (30–70 m/s): Touch and pressure
    • Aγ (15–30 m/s): Muscle spindle efferents
    • Aδ (12–30 m/s): Pain, cold, and touch

 

Since Type B fibers are NOT subdivided into α, β, and δ fibers, Option C is incorrect.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Type C fibers are small unmyelinated nerve fibers that conduct impulses at low velocities: Type C fibers are unmyelinated, slow-conducting, and carry pain and autonomic signals.

 

Option B. Type A fibers are the typically large and medium-sized myelinated fibers of spinal nerves: Type A fibers are large and myelinated, responsible for fast conduction in the nervous system.

 

Option D. A subset of Type A fibers has conduction velocity between 70–120 m/s: Aα fibers (motor and proprioception) have a conduction velocity between 70–120 m/s.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Type A fibers are large, myelinated, and fast-conducting, whereas Type C fibers are small, unmyelinated, and slow-conducting. Type B fibers are autonomic preganglionic fibers and are NOT subdivided into α, β, and δ subtypes (which only apply to Type A fibers).

questions.stem: A medical student have given a topic to present in class. The topic given to you was excitation-contraction coupling. It is a process in which muscle cells are stimulated to contract and it is followed by muscle cell relaxation. It involves the following events. Action potentialCalcium release into the cytoplasmCross-bridge cyclingCytoplasmic calcium removalDepolarization of T tubules Which of the following options lists the correct sequence of events for excitation-contraction coupling in skeletal muscle tissue?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) 1, 5, 2, 3, 4 

 

Excitation-Contraction Coupling (ECC) is the process that links the excitation of a muscle fiber (action potential) to the contraction of the muscle. The correct sequence of events in ECC in skeletal muscle is:

 

1. Action potential generation (Excitation):

 

  • An action potential is initiated at the neuromuscular junction when acetylcholine (ACh) binds to receptors on the muscle fiber membrane.
  • This depolarizes the sarcolemma, leading to an action potential in the muscle.

 

5. Depolarization of T-Tubules (Transverse Tubules):

 

  • The action potential propagates along the sarcolemma and into the T-tubules (transverse tubules).
  • This depolarization activates Dihydropyridine Receptors (DHPRs), which are voltage-sensitive calcium channels.

 

2. Calcium Release into the Cytoplasm:

 

  • DHPR activation mechanically triggers Ryanodine Receptors (RYR1) on the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR).
  • This leads to the release of Ca²⁺ from the SR into the cytoplasm, increasing intracellular calcium concentration.

 

3. Cross-Bridge Cycling (Contraction phase):

 

  • Calcium binds to troponin C, causing tropomyosin to shift, exposing binding sites on actin.
  • Myosin heads bind to actin, forming cross-bridges and generating muscle contraction via the power stroke.

 

4. Cytoplasmic Calcium Removal (Relaxation phase):

 

  • Calcium ATPase pumps (SERCA pumps) actively transport Ca²⁺ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
  • This reduces cytoplasmic calcium levels, allowing tropomyosin to cover the actin-binding sites again, leading to muscle relaxation.

 

Thus, the correct sequence is: 1 (Action Potential) → 5 (T-Tubule Depolarization) → 2 (Ca²⁺ Release) → 3 (Cross-Bridge Cycling) → 4 (Cytoplasmic Ca²⁺ Removal).

 

Educational Objective:

 

Excitation-contraction coupling involves action potential propagation along the sarcolemma, depolarization of T-tubules, calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum via ryanodine receptors, cross-bridge cycling for muscle contraction, and eventual calcium reuptake into the sarcoplasmic reticulum for relaxation.

questions.stem: All of the following are components responsible for the counter current mechanism in the kidney except:

options.label: A
options.text: Sodium outflow in thick ascending limb

options.label: B
options.text: Water outflow in thin descending limb

options.label: C
options.text: Sodium outflow in thin ascending limb

options.label: D
options.text: Flow of tubular fluid from PCT to DCT

questions.answerText: Flow of tubular fluid from PCT to DCT
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Flow of tubular fluid from PCT to DCT

 

The counter-current mechanism in the kidney relies on the Loop of Henle and vasa recta to create a concentration gradient for water reabsorption. The PCT and DCT do not participate in this process, as their primary roles are bulk reabsorption and fine-tuning electrolyte balance, respectively. Since counter-current exchange requires closely positioned limbs, the flow from PCT to DCT does not contribute to this mechanism.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Sodium outflow in thick ascending limb: The thick ascending limb actively pumps Na⁺, K⁺, and Cl⁻ out of the tubule, generating the medullary osmotic gradient.

 

Option B. Water outflow in thin descending limb: The descending limb allows passive water reabsorption, concentrating tubular fluid.

 

Option C. Sodium outflow in thin ascending limb: The thin ascending limb is impermeable to water but allows passive diffusion of Na⁺ and Cl⁻, contributing to the osmotic gradient.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The counter-current mechanism in the kidney, primarily involving the Loop of Henle and vasa recta, helps concentrate urine by creating a medullary osmotic gradient. The thick ascending limb actively pumps Na⁺ out, the thin descending limb allows water reabsorption, and the thin ascending limb allows passive sodium outflow. The PCT and DCT are not part of this system.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man met with a bike accident and handle of bike hit him badly that when he was brought to the hospital. Doctors find out that there is puncture in parietal pleura membrane. True about this condition is:

options.label: A
options.text: Unopposed inward recoil will be there.

options.label: B
options.text: Intra thorax pressure will be zero

options.label: D
options.text: Both A and B are true.

questions.answerText: Both A and B are true.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Both A and B are true.

 

Option A. Unopposed inward recoil will be there: True

 

  • The lung naturally wants to collapse due to its elastic recoil, while the chest wall wants to expand. Normally, the negative intrapleural pressure (-2.5 mmHg) prevents lung collapse.
  • In pneumothorax, when the parietal pleura is punctured, air enters the pleural space, eliminating the negative pressure.
  • This leads to unopposed lung recoil, causing lung collapse.

 

Option B. Intra-thoracic pressure will be zero: True

 

  • Since the pleural space is now connected to the atmosphere, air flows in until intra-thoracic pressure equals atmospheric pressure (0 mmHg).

 

Other Option:

 

Option C. Lungs will remain intact: False

 

  • In pneumothorax, the lung collapses due to the loss of negative intrapleural pressure.
  • The visceral pleura may remain intact, but the lung cannot function properly.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Pneumothorax occurs when the pleural space is opened to the atmosphere, causing intrapleural pressure to equalize with atmospheric pressure (0 mmHg). This eliminates the negative pressure that keeps the lung expanded, leading to lung collapse due to unopposed elastic recoil.

questions.stem: A patient with parathyroid deficiency 10 days after inadvertent damage to the parathyroid glands during thyroid surgery would probably have:

options.label: A
options.text: Low plasma phosphate and Ca2+ levels and tetanus.

options.label: B
options.text: Low plasma Ca2+ level, increased muscular excitability and spasm of the muscles.

options.label: C
options.text: High plasma phosphate and Ca2+ levels and bone demineralization.

options.label: D
options.text: Increased muscular excitability, a high plasma Ca2+ level, and bone demineralization

questions.answerText: Low plasma Ca2+ level, increased muscular excitability and spasm of the muscles.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Low plasma Ca2+ level, increased muscular excitability and spasm of the muscles.

 

  • The parathyroid gland regulates calcium and phosphate levels via parathyroid hormone (PTH).
  • PTH increases serum calcium (Ca²⁺) and decreases serum phosphate (PO₄³⁻) by promoting calcium reabsorption in the kidneys, increasing bone resorption, and stimulating vitamin D activation.
  • Inadvertent damage to the parathyroid glands during thyroid surgery leads to hypoparathyroidism, causing low plasma calcium levels (hypocalcemia) and high phosphate levels (due to reduced renal excretion).
  • Effects of hypocalcemia:
    • Increased neuromuscular excitability due to decreased calcium acting as a stabilizer for sodium channels.
    • Trousseau's sign (carpopedal spasm when a blood pressure cuff is inflated).
    • Chvostek’s sign (facial muscle twitching upon tapping the facial nerve).
    • Muscle spasms and tetany (painful involuntary muscle contractions).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Low plasma phosphate and Ca²⁺ levels and tetanus:

 

  • Plasma phosphate increases, not decreases, in hypoparathyroidism due to reduced renal excretion.
  • Tetany can occur due to hypocalcemia, but phosphate is elevated, not low.

 

Option C. High plasma phosphate and Ca²⁺ levels and bone demineralization:

 

  • Plasma calcium is low, not high.
  • Bone demineralization occurs in hyperparathyroidism, not hypoparathyroidism.

 

Option D. Increased muscular excitability, a high plasma Ca²⁺ level, and bone demineralization:

 

  • Muscular excitability is increased (correct) due to hypocalcemia, but plasma calcium is low, not high.
  • Bone demineralization occurs in hyperparathyroidism, not hypoparathyroidism.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Hypoparathyroidism leads to hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia. Low calcium increases neuromuscular excitability, causing symptoms like Trousseau’s and Chvostek’s signs, muscle spasms, and tetany.

questions.stemHtml: 43-year-old female came for the routine checkup, on investigation found out to be overweight. She was asymptomatic so just advised life style modification and decrease carbohydrate intake. Which curve in adjacent graph shows its transport of glucose across the enterocyte membrane?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) B

 

  • Glucose transport across enterocyte membranes occurs via facilitated diffusion and active transport.
  • Curve B represents facilitated diffusion, which follows a saturable, carrier-mediated transport mechanism.
  • Sodium-Glucose Linked Transporter (SGLT-1) in the small intestine mediates active transport of glucose (coupled with Na⁺) from the lumen into the enterocyte.
  • Once inside, glucose exits the enterocyte via GLUT-2 (facilitated diffusion) into the bloodstream.
  • Facilitated diffusion exhibits saturation kinetics (Vmax), as shown in curve B, unlike simple diffusion, which follows a linear pattern (Curve A).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. A:

 

  • Represents simple diffusion, which is non-saturable and does not require transport proteins.
  • Glucose is a polar, hydrophilic molecule that cannot passively diffuse across the lipid bilayer without a transporter.

 

Option C. C:

 

  • Represents active transport, which requires ATP.
  • Although glucose uptake via SGLT-1 is Na⁺-dependent, the exit into the blood (via GLUT-2) does not require ATP.

 

Option D. All of the above:

 

  • Only Curve B correctly represents glucose transport across the enterocyte via facilitated diffusion.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Glucose transport across enterocytes occurs via facilitated diffusion (GLUT-2) and sodium-dependent active transport (SGLT-1). Facilitated diffusion follows a saturable kinetics pattern (Vmax), as shown in Curve B.

questions.stem: Which of the following are secreted from the parietal cells of the stomach? MucousHydrochloric acidGastrinIntrinsic factor
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) 2, 4

 

  • The parietal cells (also known as oxyntic cells) are located in the gastric glands of the fundus and body of the stomach.
  • They secrete:

 

2. Hydrochloric acid (HCl) → Important for protein digestion, activation of pepsinogen to pepsin, and maintaining a low pH.

 

4. Intrinsic factor (IF) → Essential for vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum.

 

Other Options:

 

1. Gastrin is secreted by G-cells, not parietal cells.

 

3. Mucous is secreted by mucous cells, not parietal cells.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid (HCl) and intrinsic factor (IF), which are essential for digestion and vitamin B12 absorption, respectively. Gastrin is secreted by G-cells, while mucous is secreted by mucous cells.

questions.stem: In a child presenting with short stature, GH levels were found to be high but IGF-1 levels are low. Likely abnormality?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) GH receptor defect

 

  • Growth Hormone (GH) is secreted by the anterior pituitary in response to growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) from the hypothalamus.
  • GH acts on the liver to stimulate the production of Insulin-like Growth Factor-1 (IGF-1), which is the primary mediator of GH’s growth-promoting effects.
  • In this case:
    • GH levels are high, but IGF-1 levels are low → suggests that GH is being produced but is not exerting its effects on the liver.
    • This indicates a GH receptor defect (Laron syndrome), where the liver does not respond to GH, leading to low IGF-1 levels and short stature.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. GHRH deficiency: If GHRH was deficient, GH levels would be low, not high.

 

Option B. GHRH receptor defect: If GHRH receptor was defective, GH levels would be low, since the pituitary would not be stimulated.

 

Option D. Panhypopituitarism: In panhypopituitarism, multiple pituitary hormones would be affected, leading to low GH levels along with deficiencies in other pituitary hormones.

 

Educational Objective:

 

GH receptor defects (Laron syndrome) result in high GH levels but low IGF-1 levels, leading to growth failure. This is due to the inability of GH to act on the liver and stimulate IGF-1 production.

questions.stem: In a 30-year-old healthy male, the different body fluid compartments were measured. Which of the following can be used to measure his interstitial fluid volume?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Thiosulfate & Evan’s Blue 

 

  • Interstitial Fluid (IF) is the fluid present between the cells and is a part of the extracellular fluid (ECF).
  • Direct measurement of interstitial fluid volume is not possible, so it is calculated indirectly using the formula: Interstitial Fluid (IF)=Extracellular Fluid (ECF)−Plasma Volume
  • To measure ECF, thiosulfate (or inulin, mannitol, radioactive sodium) is used.
  • To measure plasma volume, Evan’s Blue dye (which binds to albumin) is used.

 

Thus, Thiosulfate (ECF marker) and Evan’s Blue (Plasma marker) together help in measuring Interstitial Fluid Volume (IFV).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Antipyrine & Evan’s Blue:

 

  • Antipyrine is used to measure Total Body Water (TBW), not ECF.
  • Evan’s Blue measures Plasma Volume, but without an ECF marker, IFV cannot be determined.

 

Option B. Tritium oxide & Aminopyrine:

 

  • Tritium oxide (T₂O) is a marker for Total Body Water (TBW).
  • Aminopyrine also measures TBW, not ECF.

 

Option D. Radiolabelled Albumin & Deuterium oxide:

 

  • Radiolabelled albumin measures Plasma Volume, but Deuterium oxide (D₂O) measures TBW, not ECF.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Interstitial Fluid Volume (IFV) is calculated as ECF - Plasma Volume. Thiosulfate is used to measure ECF, and Evan’s Blue is used to measure Plasma Volume.

questions.stemHtml: Difference in trajectory between inspiratory loop and the expiratory loop in the curve is due to:

options.label: A
options.text: Difference in alveolar pressure during inspiration and expiration

options.label: B
options.text: Difference in concentration of surfactant during inspiration and expiration

options.label: C
options.text: Difference in airway resistance during inspiration and expiration

options.label: D
options.text: Inspiration is active and expiration is passive

questions.answerText: Difference in concentration of surfactant during inspiration and expiration
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Difference in concentration of surfactant during inspiration and expiration 

 

  • The given graph represents hysteresis, which is the difference between the inspiratory and expiratory loops in the lung compliance curve.
  • Inspiration requires more effort (higher pressure) to expand alveoli due to surface tension created by the air-water interface inside the alveoli.
  • Surfactant (produced by Type II alveolar cells) reduces surface tension, making alveolar expansion easier.
  • During inspiration, surfactant molecules are spread out due to alveolar expansion, decreasing their concentration per unit area, which temporarily reduces lung compliance.
  • During expiration, surfactant molecules become closer together, increasing their concentration per unit area and reducing surface tension more efficiently, leading to higher compliance and easier lung deflation.
  • This difference in surfactant concentration between inspiration and expiration creates the hysteresis loop seen in the graph.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Difference in alveolar pressure during inspiration and expiration:

 

  • While alveolar pressure does change during the respiratory cycle, it does not explain the difference in compliance seen in the hysteresis loop.

 

Option C. Difference in airway resistance during inspiration and expiration:

 

  • Airway resistance affects airflow, but it is not responsible for the compliance differences observed in this curve.
  • Dynamic airway compression occurs during forced expiration, but it does not explain the shape of the hysteresis curve.

 

Option D. Inspiration is active and expiration is passive:

 

  • This is a true statement, but it does not explain the hysteresis observed in the compliance curve.
  • Hysteresis is not due to active or passive nature of breathing, but rather due to surface tension and surfactant differences.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Hysteresis in lung compliance occurs due to differences in surfactant concentration between inspiration and expiration. During inspiration, surfactant is spread out, reducing compliance, while during expiration, surfactant is concentrated, increasing compliance.

questions.stem: X, Y, Z are the three ions permeable. X =-50 and Y =-30. If at resting membrane potential (RMP), when there is no net electro genic transfer, what is the value of Z?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) +80

 

  • Given that X = -50 mV and Y = -30 mV, we are asked to find the equilibrium potential of Z when there is no net electrogenic transfer (i.e., the total sum of equilibrium potentials must be zero).
  • The equation is: X+Y+Z=0
  • Substituting the given values: 
  • −50+(−30) +Z=0
  • 80 + Z = 0
  • Z=+80

 

Thus, Z = +80 mV, making option C the correct answer.

 

Educational Objective:

 

When multiple ions contribute to the resting membrane potential, their equilibrium potentials must sum to zero if there is no net electrogenic transfer. The equilibrium potential of an unknown ion can be determined using algebraic summation.

questions.stem: Efferent arteriolar constriction causes all of the following except:

options.label: C
options.text: Increases oncotic pressure in peritubular capillaries

options.label: D
options.text: Increases hydrostatic pressure in glomerular capillaries

questions.answerText: Increases oncotic pressure in peritubular capillaries
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Increases oncotic pressure in peritubular capillaries

 

  • Efferent arteriolar constriction leads to an increase in glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure, which increases the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) initially. However, if constriction is excessive, it reduces renal blood flow (RBF), leading to a compensatory fall in GFR over time.
  • Renal blood flow (RBF) always decreases because the resistance in the efferent arteriole increases.
  • Hydrostatic pressure in glomerular capillaries increases due to restricted outflow, which enhances filtration.
  • Oncotic pressure in peritubular capillaries does NOT increase significantly because proteins are retained within the glomerular capillaries and only minimal plasma proteins enter the peritubular circulation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Decrease in GFR: Initially, GFR increases, but if constriction is excessive, protein accumulation raises oncotic pressure, opposing further filtration and decreasing GFR.

 

Option B. Decreases renal blood flow: Efferent arteriolar constriction increases vascular resistance, reducing renal blood flow (RBF) consistently.

 

Option D. Increases hydrostatic pressure in glomerular capillaries: By restricting the outflow of blood, efferent arteriolar constriction raises glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure, which initially increases GFR.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Efferent arteriolar constriction initially increases glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure, raising GFR. However, excessive constriction reduces GFR due to increased oncotic pressure. Renal blood flow always decreases.

questions.stem: A professor discusses the case of a 28-year-old woman experiencing episodic muscle weakness triggered by changes in potassium levels. The professor uses this case to explore the underlying mechanisms of positive feedback mechanism. Which component amongst the given scenario explains the phenomenon?

options.label: A
options.text: The Shell body temperature is increased after activation of thermoregulatory mechanisms such as shivering.

options.label: B
options.text: The core body temperature is maintained even if the environmental temperature is low.

options.label: C
options.text: Voltage-gated sodium channels open in response to initial depolarization, further depolarizing the membrane.

options.label: D
options.text: The heart rate increases just before starting an exercise due to psychic stimuli

questions.answerText: Voltage-gated sodium channels open in response to initial depolarization, further depolarizing the membrane.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Voltage-gated sodium channels open in response to initial depolarization, further depolarizing the membrane.

 

  • Positive feedback mechanisms amplify an initial stimulus instead of counteracting it, unlike negative feedback.
  • The opening of voltage-gated sodium (Na⁺) channels during an action potential is a classic example of positive feedback.
    • Depolarization of the membrane causes Na⁺ channels to open.
    • This leads to further Na⁺ influx, causing even more depolarization.
    • This cycle (Hodgkin cycle) continues until an inactivation mechanism (such as Na⁺ channel inactivation) terminates the response.
  • In the given case, episodic muscle weakness related to potassium changes suggests a channelopathy affecting ion channels, reinforcing the concept of voltage-gated sodium channel activation as an example of positive feedback.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. The Shell body temperature is increased after activation of thermoregulatory mechanisms such as shivering:

 

  • This is an example of negative feedback, not positive feedback.
  • Shivering increases heat production to restore normal temperature, counteracting the deviation.

 

Option B. The core body temperature is maintained even if the environmental temperature is low:

 

  • This is an example of homeostasis regulated via negative feedback, not positive feedback.
  • Temperature control mechanisms (vasoconstriction, shivering) act to maintain stability, not amplify changes.

 

Option D. The heart rate increases just before starting an exercise due to psychic stimuli:

 

  • This represents a feed-forward mechanism, not feedback (positive or negative).
  • The brain anticipates the need for increased cardiac output before physical exertion.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Positive feedback mechanisms amplify an initial change instead of counteracting it. A prime example is the Hodgkin cycle, where voltage-gated sodium channels open in response to depolarization, causing further depolarization until inactivation mechanisms intervene.

questions.stem: In a patient undergoing cancer treatment, which protein associated with Microtubule Organizing Centres (MTOCs) becomes a key target due to its crucial role in cell division, making it a promising target for chemotherapy?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Tubulin

 

  • Microtubules play a crucial role in cell division, and they are primarily composed of tubulin proteins.
  • Microtubule Organizing Centers (MTOCs), such as the centrosome, regulate microtubule polymerization and are essential for spindle fiber formation during mitosis.
  • Chemotherapeutic agents like paclitaxel (Taxol) and vincristine specifically target tubulin to disrupt microtubule dynamics, thereby preventing cancer cell proliferation.
  • By stabilizing or destabilizing microtubules, these drugs inhibit mitotic spindle formation, leading to cell cycle arrest and apoptosis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Laminin: Laminin is a glycoprotein in the extracellular matrix (ECM), crucial for cell adhesion and tissue integrity, but not directly involved in microtubule dynamics or MTOCs.

 

Option B. Keratin: Keratin is a structural protein in epithelial cells that provides mechanical strength but has no role in microtubule assembly or mitosis.

 

Option D. Ubiquitin: Ubiquitin is involved in protein degradation via the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) and plays a role in cell cycle regulation, but it does not form the structural component of MTOCs or microtubules.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Tubulin is a key component of microtubules and MTOCs, making it a prime target for chemotherapy drugs that disrupt mitotic spindle formation, thereby inhibiting cancer cell division.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old male athlete presents to the clinic with muscle cramps and weakness after intense training sessions. Investigations are focused on assessing his muscle excitation-contraction coupling mechanism. Which of the following are primarily associated with the L tubules and play a crucial role in the initiation of muscle contraction?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Ryanodine receptors

 

  • The L-tubules refer to the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR), which stores and releases calcium (Ca²⁺) for muscle contraction.
  • Ryanodine receptors (RyR) are calcium release channels located on the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) membrane.
  • They play a crucial role in excitation-contraction coupling by releasing Ca²⁺ from the SR in response to signals from the dihydropyridine receptors (DHPR) on the T-tubules.
  • Calcium release triggers actin-myosin interactions, leading to muscle contraction.
  • Mutations or dysfunction in RyR can lead to conditions like malignant hyperthermia and exercise-induced muscle weakness.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Acetylcholine receptors: Acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) are located at the neuromuscular junction (NMJ) and are involved in synaptic transmission, not in calcium release from the L-tubules.

 

Option C. Ligand-gated sodium channels: These channels help in initiating action potentials at the NMJ but do not play a direct role in calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

 

Option D. Dihydropyridine receptors: Dihydropyridine receptors (DHPR) are voltage-sensitive calcium channels on the T-tubules that interact with RyR to trigger Ca²⁺ release from the SR. However, RyR is the receptor directly responsible for Ca²⁺ release from the L-tubules.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Ryanodine receptors (RyR) on the sarcoplasmic reticulum are the primary channels responsible for releasing calcium ions, which trigger muscle contraction in the excitation-contraction coupling process.

questions.stemHtml: A guinea-pig is dissected and a portion of its intestine is fixed in the modified Dales chamber to study the effects of some drugs on intestinal contractility. A substance X was infused in the broth following which the graph comes out as depicted. Substance X most closely resembles which of these substances?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Epinephrine 

 

  • The guinea pig's intestine was placed in Dale’s chamber to assess intestinal contractility under the influence of different drugs.
  • The graph shows a decrease in tension in the intestinal muscle after infusion of Substance X.
  • Sympathetic stimulation (epinephrine) inhibits gastrointestinal smooth muscle contraction via β2-adrenergic receptor activation, leading to relaxation of intestinal muscles.
  • Since tension decreases, the most likely identity of Substance X is epinephrine, which mimics sympathetic inhibition of intestinal motility.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Acetylcholine:

 

  • Acetylcholine (ACh) stimulates muscarinic receptors (M3) in intestinal smooth muscle, leading to contraction.
  • If ACh were given, the graph would show an increase in tension instead of a decrease.

 

Option C. KCl (Potassium chloride):

 

  • KCl causes sustained depolarization and contraction of smooth muscle.
  • If KCl were infused, the graph would show increased tension rather than relaxation.

 

Option D. BaCl₂ (Barium chloride):

 

  • BaCl₂ is a smooth muscle activator that inhibits K⁺ efflux, leading to depolarization and contraction.
  • It would cause increased tension, not relaxation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Epinephrine inhibits gastrointestinal smooth muscle contraction by activating β2-adrenergic receptors, leading to decreased tension and relaxation of intestinal muscles.

Ans. D) Lipid solubility

  • D = Diffusion coefficient (depends on solubility & molecular weight)
  • A = Surface area of membrane
  • ΔP = Concentration gradient
  • T = Membrane thickness
    • For a water-insoluble (lipophilic) substance, the most important factor is its lipid solubility because it must pass through the hydrophobic lipid bilayer of the cell membrane.
    • Higher lipid solubility allows faster diffusion, while low lipid solubility prevents the molecule from penetrating the membrane efficiently.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hydrated diameter:

 

  • This applies to water-soluble substances, not water-insoluble ones.
  • Larger hydrated diameter slows diffusion through aquaporins or channels but does not govern diffusion across the lipid bilayer.

 

Option B. Molecular weight:

Educational Objective:

 

Lipid solubility is the most important factor determining the diffusibility of a water-insoluble substance across a cell membrane, as it governs its ability to pass through the lipid bilayer.

questions.stem: Weber–Fechner law is related to:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Intensity of stimulus

 

  • Weber–Fechner Law describes the relationship between stimulus intensity and perceived sensation.
  • The law states that the magnitude of a sensation (perception) is proportional to the logarithm of the intensity of the stimulus.

 

S=k log I

 

where:

 

  • S = Perceived sensation
  • I = Physical intensity of stimulus
  • k = Constant
  • This means small changes in weak stimuli are more noticeable than small changes in strong stimuli.
  • Example: If a dim light increases slightly, you notice it more than a bright light increasing by the same amount.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Number of nerve fibers: The law is not related to the number of nerve fibers but to how the brain perceives the intensity of stimulus.

 

Option B. Number of muscle fibers: This is relevant in muscle contraction and force generation, not in sensory perception.

 

Option C. Number of stimulus: The law does not describe how many stimuli occur but rather how a single stimulus is perceived based on its intensity.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Weber–Fechner Law states that the perceived intensity of a stimulus is proportional to the logarithm of its actual intensity, meaning smaller increases in weak stimuli are more noticeable than the same increase in strong stimuli.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presents to the emergency department with complaints of sudden dizziness, nausea, and a drop in blood pressure after receiving an injection for a certain medical condition. On examination, his heart rate is found to be significantly lower than usual, leading towards the Bezold-Jarisch reflex. Which of the following is responsible for this condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Serotonin

 

The Bezold-Jarisch Reflex (BJR) is a cardiovascular reflex characterized by bradycardia, hypotension, and vasodilation in response to certain triggers. It is mediated by chemoreceptors in the heart that respond to noxious stimuli such as serotonin, veratridine, and capsaicin.

 

Mechanism of the Bezold-Jarisch Reflex:

 

  1. Trigger (Serotonin, Veratridine, or Capsaicin) activates cardiac chemoreceptors.
  2. Vagal afferent nerves (C-fibers) in the heart stimulate the brainstem.
  3. This leads to an exaggerated parasympathetic (vagal) response, resulting in:
    • Bradycardia (↓ HR)
    • Hypotension (↓ BP)
    • Peripheral vasodilation
  4. This reflex is commonly observed after IV serotonin administration or in cases of inferior myocardial infarction, hemorrhage, or prolonged upright posture (vasovagal syncope).

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Histamine: Histamine causes vasodilation and hypotension, but it does not trigger the Bezold-Jarisch Reflex. It is more related to allergic reactions and anaphylaxis.

 

Option C. Prostaglandin: Prostaglandins are vasoactive molecules that regulate inflammation, fever, and vasodilation, but they do not induce BJR.

 

Option D. Angiotensin: Angiotensin II is a vasoconstrictor and would cause hypertension and tachycardia, the opposite effect of BJR.

 

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Bezold-Jarisch Reflex is a paradoxical cardiovascular reflex caused by cardiac chemoreceptor activation (by serotonin, veratridine, or capsaicin), leading to bradycardia, hypotension, and vasodilation via vagal activation.

questions.stem: How an electrical synapse is different from a chemical synapse?

options.label: A
options.text: No cytoplasmic continuity between presynaptic and post synaptic space in electric synapses.

options.label: B
options.text: Direction of impulse is unidirectional in electric synapses.

options.label: C
options.text: Connexons are present in electrical synapse

options.label: D
options.text: Electrical synapse has more latent period than chemical synapse

questions.answerText: Connexons are present in electrical synapse
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Connexons are present in electrical synapse

 

Electrical synapses are specialized connections between neurons that allow direct ion flow via gap junctions, which consist of connexons. These connexons bridge the cytoplasm of adjacent neurons, facilitating rapid and bidirectional transmission of electrical signals.

 

Key Features of Electrical Synapses:

 

  • Cytoplasmic Continuity: Unlike chemical synapses, electrical synapses have direct cytoplasmic connections via connexons, allowing for fast impulse conduction.
  • Bidirectional Transmission: Electrical signals can travel in both directions, unlike chemical synapses which are mostly unidirectional.
  • No Synaptic Delay: Unlike chemical synapses, electrical synapses have minimal synaptic delay, making them faster and suitable for reflex circuits.
  • Present in Cardiac and Smooth Muscle: Electrical synapses are common in cardiac muscle (for synchronized contraction via intercalated discs) and some areas of the CNS.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. No cytoplasmic continuity between presynaptic and post synaptic space in electric synapses:

 

  • Electrical synapses DO have cytoplasmic continuity through connexons, allowing for direct ion flow.
  • Chemical synapses lack cytoplasmic continuity and rely on neurotransmitters.

 

Option B. Direction of impulse is unidirectional in electric synapses: Electrical synapses are bidirectional, unlike chemical synapses which are mostly unidirectional.

 

Option D. Electrical synapse has more latent period than chemical synapse:

 

  • Chemical synapses have a greater latent period because neurotransmitter release, receptor binding, and signal transduction take time.
  • Electrical synapses have almost no synaptic delay, making them faster.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Electrical synapses allow fast, bidirectional impulse conduction via connexons (gap junctions) and have minimal synaptic delay, unlike chemical synapses which rely on neurotransmitter release.
