questions.stemHtml: A 75-year-old male with a history of coronary artery disease is undergoing a routine echocardiogram that shows a normal aortic pressure waveform and the timing of coronary blood flow during the cardiac cycle. At which point on the aortic pressure waveform diagram provided is the coronary blood flow is the greatest?

options.label: A
options.text: Point B, when the aortic valve is open and the blood is being ejected into the aorta.

options.label: B
options.text: Point C, at the peak of systolic pressure within the aorta.

options.label: C
options.text: Point D, during the closing of the aortic valve.

options.label: D
options.text: Point E, in the phase of isovolumic relaxation.

questions.answerText: Point E, in the phase of isovolumic relaxation.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Point E, in the phase of isovolumic relaxation. 

 

Coronary blood flow occurs primarily during diastole, unlike other organs where blood flow is maximal during systole. This is because during systole, the contraction of the heart muscle compresses the coronary vessels, reducing perfusion. During diastole, when the heart relaxes, coronary blood flow is restored.

 

Key Phases of the Cardiac Cycle & Coronary Blood Flow:

 

  1. Systole (Point B & C):
    • The left ventricle contracts and ejects blood into the aorta.
    • The coronary arteries are compressed, limiting blood flow.
    • Minimal coronary perfusion occurs during this phase.
  2. Early Diastole (Point D - Aortic Valve Closing):
    • The aortic valve closes, and blood is momentarily held in the aorta.
    • Coronary perfusion begins to increase as compression subsides.
  3. Isovolumetric Relaxation (Point E):
    • Maximum coronary blood flow occurs.
    • The ventricles relax, and aortic pressure drives blood into the coronary arteries.
    • This phase represents the peak of diastolic coronary perfusion.

 

Thus, Point E (isovolumic relaxation) is the phase where coronary blood flow is highest because the myocardium relaxes, allowing unobstructed perfusion.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Point B (Aortic Valve Open, Ejection):

 

  • This is the phase of rapid ejection when the ventricle is forcefully contracting.
  • Coronary perfusion is minimal because the intraventricular pressure is high, compressing the coronary arteries.

 

Option B. Point C (Peak of Systolic Pressure):

 

  • Peak systolic pressure further compresses the coronary arteries.
  • This phase reduces coronary blood flow rather than increasing it.

 

Option C. Point D (Aortic Valve Closing):

 

  • Coronary flow starts to increase, but it is not at its maximum yet.
  • The best phase for coronary perfusion is Point E (isovolumic relaxation).

 

Educational Objective:

 

Coronary blood flow is highest during diastole, particularly during isovolumic relaxation, as the myocardium relaxes and the compressed coronary arteries open, allowing maximal perfusion.

questions.stemHtml: A 27-year-old man is breathing quietly. He then inhales as much air as possible and exhales as much air as he can, producing the spirogram shown in the previous figure. What is his inspiratory capacity (in liters)?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) 3.0

 

The Inspiratory Capacity (IC) is the maximum volume of air a person can inhale after a normal tidal expiration. It is calculated using the formula:

 

IC=Tidal Volume (TV)+Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV)

 

From the spirogram:

 

  • Tidal Volume (TV): The small waves represent normal quiet breathing. This is around 0.5 L.
  • Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV): This is the additional volume of air inhaled after normal inspiration.
  • The maximum inspiratory volume in the graph reaches about 6.0 L.
  • The resting lung volume (before deep inhalation) is about 3.0 L.

 

Thus,

 

IC=6.0L−3.0L=3.0L

 

Educational Objective:

 

Inspiratory Capacity (IC) is the sum of Tidal Volume (TV) and Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV) and represents the maximum amount of air that can be inhaled after a normal exhalation. It is measured from the resting expiratory level to the peak of maximum inspiration.

questions.stem: In a discussion about the factors affecting oxygen delivery to tissues, the variations in the oxygen dissociation curve are being reviewed. Which of the following conditions regarding these variations is incorrectly matched. All the following conditions regarding the variations in the oxygen dissociation curve are correctly matched, except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Increased pCO2 – left shift

 

The oxygen dissociation curve describes the relationship between the partial pressure of oxygen (pO₂) and oxygen saturation (SaO₂) in hemoglobin. Various factors can shift this curve to the right (decreased oxygen affinity) or to the left (increased oxygen affinity).

 

Mnemonic for Right Shift: "RIGHT TAG"

 

  • T - Temperature ↑
  • A - Acid (H⁺) ↑
  • G - Glycolysis (2,3-BPG) ↑
  • pCO₂ ↑ (Bohr Effect)

 

A right shift means oxygen unloading is enhanced, which is beneficial in tissues requiring more oxygen (e.g., muscles during exercise).
A left shift means oxygen is bound more tightly, making oxygen unloading to tissues harder.

 

Increased pCO₂ – Left Shift (Incorrect) 

 

  • Higher pCO₂ shifts the curve RIGHT (Bohr Effect), facilitating oxygen release to tissues.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Increased pH – Left Shift: Correct. Higher pH (less H⁺) decreases oxygen unloading, shifting the curve left.

 

Option C. Increased Temperature – Right Shift: Correct. Higher metabolic activity increases temperature, reducing hemoglobin's affinity for O₂ (right shift).

 

Option D. Increased H⁺ – Right Shift: Correctly. More H⁺ (lower pH) promotes oxygen unloading (right shift).

 

Educational Objective:

 

An increase in pCO₂, H⁺ (decreased pH), temperature, or 2,3-BPG leads to a right shift in the oxygen dissociation curve, enhancing oxygen delivery to tissues (Bohr Effect). Conversely, decreased pCO₂, H⁺, temperature, or 2,3-BPG causes a left shift, increasing hemoglobin’s affinity for oxygen.

questions.stemHtml: In a respiratory clinic, a 45-year-old non-smoker presents with a 6-month history of progressive dyspnea and a nonproductive cough. Physical examination reveals digital clubbing and fine basilar inspiratory crackles. The resulting loop resembles the image provided. Given the patient's symptoms and the flow-volume loop findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis

 

Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) is a type of restrictive lung disease characterized by progressive fibrosis of the lung interstitium. Patients often present with chronic progressive dyspnea and a nonproductive cough, along with fine inspiratory crackles on auscultation and digital clubbing.

 

Flow-Volume Loop Interpretation:

 

  • The provided flow-volume loop demonstrates a restriction pattern with a decreased total lung capacity (TLC) and forced vital capacity (FVC), which is a hallmark of restrictive lung diseases.
  • In restrictive lung disease, the loop appears smaller in size but maintains a relatively normal shape, indicating reduced lung volumes without obstructive changes.
  • The mnemonic "Right TAG" helps recall factors affecting the oxygen dissociation curve (Temperature, Acid, Glycolysis), but in terms of pulmonary function tests, restrictive lung diseases shift the graph inward due to decreased lung compliance.

 

Given the patient’s history of progressive symptoms, clubbing, inspiratory crackles, and the restrictive flow-volume loop pattern, Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis is the most likely diagnosis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Chronic Bronchitis:

 

  • Chronic bronchitis is a subtype of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and is characterized by a chronic productive cough lasting at least 3 months per year for at least 2 consecutive years.
  • It presents with an obstructive pattern on pulmonary function tests, where the expiratory limb of the flow-volume loop appears scooped out due to increased airway resistance.
  • The absence of productive cough and the presence of restrictive changes in the flow-volume loop make chronic bronchitis unlikely.

 

Option C. Asthma:

 

  • Asthma is an obstructive lung disease marked by episodic wheezing, reversible airflow obstruction, and bronchial hyperreactivity.
  • The hallmark pulmonary function test finding in asthma is a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio with a concave expiratory loop due to airflow limitation.
  • Since this patient has no wheezing, no reversible airflow obstruction, and the flow-volume loop suggests restriction rather than obstruction, asthma is not the correct diagnosis.

 

Option D. Vocal Cord Dysfunction:

 

  • Vocal cord dysfunction is a condition in which paradoxical vocal cord motion leads to episodic inspiratory airway obstruction, often mimicking asthma.
  • The characteristic flow-volume loop finding in vocal cord dysfunction is flattening of the inspiratory limb, indicating variable extrathoracic obstruction.
  • Since the provided flow-volume loop does not show this pattern and the patient has crackles and clubbing (suggestive of interstitial lung disease), vocal cord dysfunction is unlikely.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) is a restrictive lung disease characterized by progressive dyspnea, fine inspiratory crackles, and digital clubbing. Pulmonary function tests show a restrictive pattern with reduced TLC and FVC, and the flow-volume loop appears smaller but maintains a normal shape.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old patient is experiencing difficulty in consolidating short-term memories into long-term memories, leading to recurrent forgetfulness. The clinician evaluates the patient's neurological function, focusing on structures crucial for memory conversion. In a patient with difficulty in storage of long-term memories after conversion from short term memories, which brain structure plays a crucial role in this process?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Neocortex

 

Memory formation and consolidation involve multiple brain structures working in coordination. The hippocampus is responsible for converting short-term memories into long-term memories, but long-term storage primarily occurs in the neocortex.

 

  • In this case, the patient has difficulty in storing long-term memories after conversion from short-term memory. Since the conversion process itself is intact, the hippocampus is not the issue.
  • The neocortex is the brain structure responsible for long-term memory storage, integrating and organizing information for retrieval over extended periods.

 

Process of Memory Formation:

 

  1. Encoding – The process of receiving sensory input and forming short-term memories, largely involving the prefrontal cortex.
  2. Consolidation – The hippocampus plays a crucial role in converting short-term memories into long-term memories.
  3. Storage – Long-term memories are stored in the neocortex, particularly in the temporal and association cortices.

 

Since this patient’s conversion of short-term memory to long-term memory is normal, but the storage is impaired, the neocortex is the most likely affected structure.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Thalamus:

 

  • The thalamus is involved in sensory processing and relay but does not play a primary role in memory storage.
  • While the thalamus contributes to attention and consciousness, it does not store long-term memories or directly consolidate short-term memories into long-term memories.

 

Option B. Hippocampus:

 

  • The hippocampus is critical for memory consolidation, meaning it is responsible for converting short-term memories into long-term memories.
  • However, this patient has no issues with conversion, only storage, making hippocampal dysfunction unlikely.
  • Damage to the hippocampus would cause anterograde amnesia, where new memories cannot be formed, but previously stored memories remain intact.

 

Option C. Cingulate Gyrus:

 

  • The cingulate gyrus is associated with emotionally significant memory formation and attention, not the primary storage of long-term memories.
  • It helps with associative learning (e.g., remembering words, emotional aspects of memory), but does not function as the main storage center for memories.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Long-term memory storage primarily occurs in the neocortex, while the hippocampus is responsible for converting short-term memories into long-term ones. Damage to the neocortex can impair long-term memory storage without affecting initial memory formation.

questions.stem: A patient with a kidney-related concern is undergoing an evaluation. The healthcare provider discusses the characteristics and functions of juxtamedullary nephrons, including their role in urine concentration and the unique features that distinguish them from cortical nephrons. Which of the following is true about the juxtamedullary nephrons? Vasa recta well developedShort loop of Henle15% of nephronsThick and thin ascending loops
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) 1, 3, 4

 

Juxtamedullary nephrons are a specialized type of nephron that play a crucial role in urine concentration by establishing a strong osmotic gradient in the medullary interstitium.

 

1. Vasa recta well developed: True.

 

  • The vasa recta is an extensive capillary network that surrounds the loop of Henle in juxtamedullary nephrons.
  • It helps in maintaining the countercurrent exchange system, which is essential for urine concentration and water reabsorption.

 

3. 15% of nephrons: True.

 

  • Juxtamedullary nephrons make up approximately 15% of all nephrons in the kidney.
  • The remaining 85% are cortical nephrons, which have a much shorter loop of Henle and function primarily in filtration rather than concentration.

 

4. Thick and thin ascending loops: True.

 

  • The ascending limb of the loop of Henle in juxtamedullary nephrons has both a thin and thick segment.
  • The thin ascending limb is permeable to solutes but not water, contributing to the countercurrent multiplier effect.
  • The thick ascending limb actively reabsorbs Na+, K+, and Cl-, further enhancing the osmotic gradient in the medulla.

 

Thus, the correct set of characteristics includes 1, 3, and 4, making option C the correct answer.

 

Other Options:

 

2. Short loop of Henle: False.

 

  • Juxtamedullary nephrons have a long loop of Henle that extends deep into the medulla, unlike cortical nephrons, which have a short loop.
  • This deep extension is vital for generating the high osmotic gradient required for water reabsorption and concentrated urine formation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Juxtamedullary nephrons comprise about 15% of all nephrons and play a crucial role in urine concentration. They have a well-developed vasa recta, a long loop of Henle that extends deep into the medulla, and both thick and thin ascending limbs to aid in countercurrent multiplication and water reabsorption.

questions.stemHtml: A nephrologist is explaining to medical students the concept of renal clearance and how different substances are handled by the nephron. Using the graph provided, she asks them to match substances with their typical clearance patterns. Identify the correctly matched pair of substances with their renal clearance from the graph:

options.label: A
options.text: A - Glucose, B - PAH, C - Bicarbonate, D - Inulin

options.label: B
options.text: A - Bicarbonate, B - Glucose, C Inulin -, D – PAH

options.label: C
options.text: A - PAH, B - Inulin, C - Glucose, D - Bicarbonate

options.label: D
options.text: A - Glucose, B - Bicarbonate, C - Inulin, D - PAH

questions.answerText: A - Glucose, B - Bicarbonate, C - Inulin, D - PAH
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) A - Glucose, B - Bicarbonate, C - Inulin, D – PAH

 

The graph represents the percentage of a filtered load of different substances remaining along the length of the nephron. Understanding how various substances are reabsorbed or secreted is key to identifying them on the graph.

 

Analysis of Graph:

 

  1. Curve A - Glucose (Completely Reabsorbed)
    • The curve representing substance A shows a rapid decline to nearly 0% early in the nephron.
    • This is characteristic of glucose, which is actively reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) via SGLT (sodium-glucose transporters) and GLUT transporters.
    • Under normal physiological conditions, glucose is fully reabsorbed, provided the renal threshold is not exceeded (as in diabetes mellitus).
  2. Curve B - Bicarbonate (Mostly Reabsorbed)
    • Bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) is also heavily reabsorbed, but not as rapidly as glucose.
    • The proximal tubule reabsorbs around 85% of bicarbonate, and the remaining portion is fine-tuned by the collecting duct.
    • Unlike glucose, a small fraction of bicarbonate may be lost in the urine, explaining why substance B is not reabsorbed as quickly or completely as glucose.
  3. Curve C - Inulin (Freely Filtered, Not Reabsorbed or Secreted)
    • Inulin is a substance that is freely filtered at the glomerulus and neither reabsorbed nor secreted.
    • This results in a flat line on the graph (Curve C), indicating that its concentration in the filtrate remains constant as it passes through the nephron.
    • Because inulin is only cleared by filtration, it is used to measure glomerular filtration rate (GFR).
  4. Curve D - PAH (Para-Aminohippuric Acid, Secreted)
    • PAH is both filtered and actively secreted in the proximal tubule, resulting in an increase in its concentration along the nephron.
    • This accounts for the rising curve (Curve D) as more PAH is secreted into the tubule.
    • PAH is almost completely cleared from the plasma in a single pass through the kidney, making it useful for measuring renal plasma flow (RPF).

 

Thus, the correct matching is:

 

  • A - Glucose (completely reabsorbed)
  • B - Bicarbonate (mostly reabsorbed, but some remains)
  • C - Inulin (freely filtered, not reabsorbed or secreted)
  • D - PAH (filtered and secreted, leading to increasing concentration)

 

Educational Objective:

 

Glucose is completely reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, bicarbonate is mostly reabsorbed but can be lost in small amounts, inulin is freely filtered but not reabsorbed or secreted (used to measure GFR), and PAH is both filtered and secreted, making it a marker for renal plasma flow.

questions.stem: A medical student is studying thyroid physiology and comes across the term 'Wolf-Chaikoff effect.' She is curious about the mechanism underlying this phenomenon. Which of the following best explains the Wolf-Chaikoff effect?
questions.solutionHtml:
ct answer.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Suppression of TSH secretion:

 

  • The Wolff-Chaikoff effect is a direct effect on the thyroid gland itself and does not act through TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone).
  • In fact, due to the temporary drop in T3 and T4 levels, TSH levels may actually increase as a compensatory mechanism.

 

Option C. Decreased T3 to T4 conversion:

 

  • The Wolff-Chaikoff effect is not related to peripheral conversion of T4 to T3.
  • T3 is converted from T4 mainly in the liver and peripheral tissues via deiodinase enzymes, which are unaffected by the direct thyroidal effects of excessive iodine intake.

 

Option D. Excessive iodine intake – Partially Correct but Not the Best Answer

 

  • While excessive iodine intake is the cause of the Wolff-Chaikoff effect, it does not directly explain the mechanism.
  • The actual mechanism is the decrease in iodination of MIT and DIT, which reduces thyroid hormone synthesis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Wolff-Chaikoff effect describes the transient inhibition of thyroid hormone synthesis due to excessive iodine intake. This occurs due to decreased iodination of tyrosine residues (MIT and DIT) in thyroglobulin, mediated by the suppression of thyroid peroxidase (TPO).

questions.stem: In response to an increase in GFR, the proximal tubule and the loop of Henle demonstrate an increase in the rate of Na+ reabsorption. This phenomenon is called?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Glomerulo tubular balance 

 

Glomerulo tubular balance (GT balance) is a regulatory mechanism that ensures a constant fraction of sodium (Na⁺) and water is reabsorbed from the proximal tubule despite fluctuations in glomerular filtration rate (GFR).

 

Mechanism of Glomerulo tubular Balance:

 

  • When GFR increases, proximal tubular Na⁺ reabsorption also increases proportionally, maintaining a constant fractional reabsorption (typically ~65-70% of filtered Na⁺).
  • This balance is primarily maintained by changes in peritubular capillary oncotic pressure and tubular flow rate.
  • Similarly, if GFR decreases, Na⁺ reabsorption also decreases, ensuring homeostasis.

 

Thus, glomerulo tubular balance helps prevent excessive sodium and water loss or retention, stabilizing fluid balance in the kidneys.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Autoregulation:

 

  • Autoregulation refers to the intrinsic ability of the kidneys to maintain a stable GFR despite changes in systemic blood pressure.
  • It involves mechanisms such as the myogenic response and tubulo glomerular feedback, but it does not describe the proportional adjustment of sodium reabsorption in response to GFR changes.

 

Option C. Mineralocorticoid Escape:

 

  • Mineralocorticoid escape occurs in hyperaldosteronism (e.g., Conn’s syndrome), where despite excess aldosterone causing Na⁺ retention, edema does not develop due to compensatory mechanisms like increased atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) secretion.
  • This phenomenon is not related to glomerulo tubular balance.

 

Option D. Saturation of Tubular Transport:

 

  • Saturation of tubular transport occurs when a solute’s reabsorption reaches its maximum capacity (Tm), as seen in conditions like diabetes mellitus, where glucose transporters become overwhelmed.
  • This is a transport limitation phenomenon, not a homeostatic regulatory process like glomerulotubular balance.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Glomerulo tubular balance ensures that the proximal tubule reabsorbs a constant fraction of Na⁺ and water despite changes in GFR. This prevents excessive sodium loss or retention, contributing to renal homeostasis.

questions.stem: Which one of the following clinical disorder specifically arises due to the defective functioning of aquaporins, notably AQP2, crucial for water reabsorption in the kidney tubules, which disrupts the kidney's ability to concentrate urine, resulting in a distinctive pattern of excessive urine output, thirst, and potential dehydration despite adequate fluid intake:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Nephrogenic DI

 

Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus (DI) is a disorder characterized by impaired water reabsorption in the collecting ducts of the kidney due to the defective functioning of aquaporin-2 (AQP2) channels.

 

Mechanism:

 

  1. Aquaporin-2 (AQP2) channels are responsible for water reabsorption in the collecting duct, under the regulation of antidiuretic hormone (ADH or vasopressin).
  2. In Nephrogenic DI, the kidneys fail to respond to ADH, leading to:
    • Impaired water reabsorption
    • Excessive dilute urine output (polyuria)
    • Intense thirst (polydipsia)
    • Risk of dehydration despite adequate fluid intake
  3. Causes of Nephrogenic DI:
    • Genetic mutations in AQP2 or V2 receptor (X-linked)
    • Lithium toxicity (common acquired cause)
    • Hypercalcemia, hypokalemia

 

Since AQP2 dysfunction is central to the pathogenesis of Nephrogenic DI, option A is the correct answer.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Liddle Syndrome:

 

  • Liddle syndrome is caused by a gain-of-function mutation in the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC), leading to excessive sodium reabsorption in the distal tubule.
  • It presents with hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and low aldosterone levels, not polyuria or water loss.
  • AQP2 is not involved in Liddle syndrome.

 

Option C. Von Hippel-Lindau Syndrome:

 

  • This is a genetic disorder affecting the VHL tumor suppressor gene, leading to tumors and cysts in multiple organs, including the kidneys.
  • It does not involve AQP2 dysfunction or cause diabetes insipidus.

 

Option D. Bartter Syndrome:

 

  • Bartter syndrome is caused by mutations affecting the sodium-potassium-2-chloride (NKCC2) cotransporter in the loop of Henle.
  • It leads to hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and polyuria, but the mechanism is not related to AQP2.
  • The main defect is in sodium reabsorption, not water reabsorption via aquaporins.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus (DI) results from defective AQP2 function, leading to impaired water reabsorption, polyuria, polydipsia, and dehydration. Unlike central DI, nephrogenic DI does not respond to ADH treatment.

questions.stemHtml: During starvation, graph of three substances are plotted as below. The scale for A and B is on the left and the scale for C is on the right. Which of the substances are represented by the curve A?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) RT3 

 

During starvation, the body reduces metabolism to conserve energy. This is achieved through thyroid hormone regulation, specifically affecting T3 and reverse T3 (RT3) levels.

 

Key Thyroid Hormone Changes During Starvation:

 

  1. T4 (Thyroxine) levels (Curve B)
    • T4 levels remain relatively stable, decreasing only mildly (~20-30%).
    • This is because T4 is the inactive precursor and is not directly responsible for metabolic rate changes.
  2. T3 (Triiodothyronine) levels (Curve C)
    • T3 is the active thyroid hormone responsible for metabolism.
    • During starvation, T3 levels drop significantly because reducing metabolism helps conserve energy.
    • The body converts less T4 into T3, shifting towards an alternative pathway.
  3. Reverse T3 (RT3) levels (Curve A)
    • RT3 is an inactive form of T3 produced when T4 is diverted away from forming active T3.
    • During starvation, RT3 levels increase significantly to further suppress metabolic rate, helping in energy conservation.
    • This explains why Curve A is rising—indicating increasing RT3 levels.

 

Thus, curve A represents Reverse T3 (RT3), making option A the correct answer.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Thyroxine (T4):

 

  • T4 (Curve B) remains relatively stable, with only a slight decrease (~20-30%).
  • Since A is increasing, it cannot represent T4.

 

Option C. Triiodothyronine (T3):

 

  • T3 (Curve C) decreases, as the body suppresses metabolism during starvation.
  • A is increasing, but T3 decreases, making this answer incorrect.

 

Option D. Diiodotyrosine (DIT):

 

  • DIT is an intermediate in thyroid hormone synthesis, not a major hormone that fluctuates significantly during starvation.
  • It is not plotted in metabolic studies related to starvation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

During starvation, the body conserves energy by decreasing T3 levels and increasing RT3 levels. Reverse T3 (RT3) is an inactive thyroid hormone that rises significantly in fasting states to suppress metabolic rate.

questions.stem: Which one of the following statement accurately describes the a neurological phenomenon commonly observed in motor control and pivotal in maintaining appropriate muscle tension, involves a specific neuronal pathway with interneuronal processing between sensory and motor neurons, regulating muscle contraction by modulating motor neuron activity based on Golgi tendon organ input:

options.label: A
options.text: Occurs when IA spindle afferents are inhibited.

options.label: B
options.text: Is a monosynaptic reflex initiated by activation of the Golgi tendon organ.

options.label: C
options.text: Is a disynaptic reflex with a single interneuron inserted between the afferent and efferent limbs.

options.label: D
options.text: Uses type II afferent fibers from the Golgi tendon organ

questions.answerText: Is a disynaptic reflex with a single interneuron inserted between the afferent and efferent limbs.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Is a disynaptic reflex with a single interneuron inserted between the afferent and efferent limbs. 

 

This question describes the inverse stretch reflex (Golgi tendon reflex), a protective mechanism that prevents excessive muscle tension by causing muscle relaxation when the Golgi tendon organ (GTO) is excessively stimulated.

 

Mechanism of the Golgi Tendon Reflex:

 

  1. Golgi Tendon Organs (GTOs), located at the junction of muscles and tendons, sense excessive muscle tension.
  2. When tension increases too much, Ib afferent fibers from the GTO send signals to the spinal cord.
  3. These Ib afferents synapse on an inhibitory interneuron in the spinal cord.
  4. The interneuron then inhibits the alpha motor neuron, leading to muscle relaxation to prevent damage from excessive force.
  5. Because this pathway includes an interneuron, it is classified as a disynaptic reflex (two synapses: Ib afferent → interneuron → motor neuron).

 

Thus, the correct answer is C, as the Golgi tendon reflex is a disynaptic reflex with one inhibitory interneuron between the sensory and motor neurons.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Occurs when IA spindle afferents are inhibited:

 

  • IA afferent fibers come from muscle spindles, which are involved in the stretch reflex (not the Golgi tendon reflex).
  • The stretch reflex is monosynaptic and leads to muscle contraction, whereas the Golgi tendon reflex leads to relaxation.

 

Option B. Is a monosynaptic reflex initiated by activation of the Golgi tendon organ:

 

  • Monosynaptic reflexes do not involve interneurons (e.g., the stretch reflex).
  • The Golgi tendon reflex is disynaptic, requiring an interneuron to inhibit the motor neuron.

 

Option D. Uses type II afferent fibers from the Golgi tendon organ:

 

  • Type II afferents are involved in muscle spindle activity, particularly in sensing static muscle length, and are not related to the Golgi tendon reflex.
  • The Golgi tendon organ uses Ib afferent fibers, not type II afferents.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Golgi tendon reflex (inverse stretch reflex) is a disynaptic reflex that prevents excessive muscle tension. It involves the Golgi tendon organ (GTO), which sends signals via Ib afferents to an inhibitory interneuron, leading to muscle relaxation.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old male patient presents with symptoms of excessive urination, extreme thirst, and unexplained weight loss over the past few months. Laboratory investigations reveal hyperglycemia and ketonuria. During the investigation of signaling pathways involved in various hormones, Which hormone, in this case of the patient's symptoms suggesting diabetes mellitus, differs from the others by not utilizing cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) as its second messenger system in intracellular signaling pathways?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Prolactin

 

The cAMP (cyclic adenosine monophosphate) second messenger system is a common intracellular signaling pathway used by many hormones to mediate their effects.

 

  • Hormones that use cAMP typically bind to G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) and activate adenylate cyclase, leading to cAMP production and activation of protein kinase A (PKA) for downstream effects.
  • Prolactin, however, does not use cAMP; instead, it signals through the JAK-STAT (Janus kinase-signal transducer and activator of transcription) pathway, a cytokine receptor-mediated mechanism.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Corticotropin (ACTH):

 

  • ACTH (Adrenocorticotropic Hormone) uses the cAMP pathway via GPCR activation in the adrenal cortex to stimulate cortisol production.
  • It binds to the melanocortin 2 receptor (MC2R) on adrenal cells, triggering adenylate cyclase to increase cAMP levels.

 

Option B. Dopamine:

 

  • Dopamine acts through GPCRs, specifically D1 receptors (stimulatory, increase cAMP) and D2 receptors (inhibitory, decrease cAMP).
  • While D2 receptor activation decreases cAMP, dopamine signaling still involves the cAMP system.

 

Option C. Glucagon:

 

  • Glucagon signals via the cAMP pathway, binding to GPCRs on hepatocytes and activating adenylate cyclase.
  • This leads to an increase in cAMP levels, stimulating glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, which is crucial in diabetes mellitus.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Prolactin differs from other hormones like ACTH, Dopamine, and Glucagon because it does not use the cAMP second messenger system. Instead, Prolactin signals through the JAK-STAT pathway, which is characteristic of cytokine receptor signaling.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old female patient experiencing irregular menstrual cycles and seeking guidance from her healthcare provider. During the healthcare team explores factors influencing reproductive hormone regulation. Which of the following have a role in controlling the secretion of Prolactin?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Dopamine

 

Prolactin secretion from the anterior pituitary is primarily regulated by dopamine, which acts as the prolactin-inhibiting factor (PIF).

 

Mechanism of Prolactin Regulation:

 

  1. Dopamine (Prolactin-Inhibiting Hormone - PIH) from the hypothalamus inhibits prolactin release via D2 receptors in the anterior pituitary.
  2. If dopamine levels decrease, prolactin secretion increases, which is why pituitary stalk damage or dopamine antagonists (e.g., antipsychotics) lead to hyperprolactinemia.
  3. Prolactin itself has a negative feedback effect, stimulating dopamine release to maintain balance.

 

Thus, dopamine is the primary regulator of prolactin secretion.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Serotonin:

 

  • Serotonin (5-HT) stimulates prolactin release, but it is not the primary regulator.
  • Serotonergic drugs (e.g., SSRIs) can cause mild prolactin elevation, but dopamine inhibition remains the dominant regulatory mechanism.

 

Option B. GABA:

 

  • GABA does not directly regulate prolactin secretion in a significant way.
  • It has minor indirect effects on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis, but dopamine remains the primary regulator.

 

Option C. Somatostatin:

 

  • Somatostatin primarily inhibits growth hormone (GH) and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH).
  • While it can modulate prolactin secretion indirectly, it is not a major factor in prolactin control.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Dopamine is the primary inhibitory regulator of prolactin secretion. A decrease in dopamine (due to pituitary stalk damage, dopamine antagonists, or hypothalamic dysfunction) leads to increased prolactin levels, which can cause hyperprolactinemia and associated symptoms like menstrual irregularities and galactorrhea.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old patient undergoing evaluation for a suspected catecholamine-secreting tumor The healthcare team, into a comprehensive discussion on the principal metabolite resulting from norepinephrine metabolism and subsequently excreted in urine and the clinical implications of measuring this metabolite in the context of diagnosing and managing catecholamine-secreting tumors. The metabolite is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Vanillyl Mandelic Acid (VMA)

 

Catecholamine-secreting tumors, such as pheochromocytoma, produce excess epinephrine, norepinephrine, and dopamine. These catecholamines are metabolized and excreted in the urine as specific metabolites.

 

Metabolic Pathway of Catecholamines:

 

  1. Norepinephrine & Epinephrine → Metanephrines (via Catechol-O-Methyltransferase, COMT)
  2. Metanephrines → Vanillyl-Mandelic Acid (VMA) (via Monoamine Oxidase, MAO)
  3. VMA is the final excreted product in urine, making it the best metabolite for diagnosing pheochromocytoma.

 

Why VMA is Clinically Important?

 

  • VMA is a stable end-product of catecholamine metabolism.
  • It remains detectable in urine for an extended period, unlike metanephrines, which degrade more quickly.
  • Urinary VMA levels are a crucial diagnostic marker for pheochromocytoma and other catecholamine-producing tumors.

 

Thus, the correct answer is Vanillyl-Mandelic Acid (VMA), making option D the correct choice.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Metanephrine:

 

  • Metanephrines are intermediate metabolites of catecholamine metabolism.
  • While they are useful in plasma-based screening, urinary VMA is more reliable for long-term assessment.

 

Option B. Homogentisic Acid:

 

  • Homogentisic acid is a metabolite of tyrosine, not catecholamines.
  • Its accumulation is associated with alkaptonuria, a metabolic disorder.

 

Option C. Aspartic Acid:

 

  • Aspartic acid is an amino acid, unrelated to catecholamine metabolism.
  • It plays a role in neurotransmission but is not used for pheochromocytoma diagnosis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Vanillyl-Mandelic Acid (VMA) is the principal urinary metabolite of norepinephrine metabolism and is a key diagnostic marker for catecholamine-secreting tumors like pheochromocytoma. Measuring urinary VMA helps in confirming excessive catecholamine production.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old patient with a history of osteoporosis is undergoing a comprehensive evaluation of calcium metabolism. Understanding the dynamics of the active form of calcium can help in tailoring interventions to address the patient's osteoporosis and prevent further bone loss, considering both pharmacological and lifestyle-based approaches. The active form of calcium in body is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Ionized calcium

 

Ionized calcium is the physiologically active form of calcium in the body. It is not bound to proteins or other molecules, making it readily available for biological functions such as neuromuscular excitability, blood coagulation, and bone metabolism. The body's calcium homeostasis is tightly regulated by parathyroid hormone (PTH), vitamin D, and calcitonin, which influence the levels of ionized calcium in the blood.

 

When calcium binds to albumin or forms complexes with phosphate or oxalates, it is not readily available for immediate physiological functions. Therefore, ionized calcium represents the biologically active form that directly participates in critical physiological processes.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Complexed with Phosphate: Calcium bound to phosphate forms insoluble salts, which play a role in bone mineralization but are not immediately available for metabolic functions.

 

Option C. Complexed with Oxalates: Calcium oxalate is an insoluble compound often excreted through urine and associated with kidney stones rather than playing an active role in calcium homeostasis.

 

Option D. Bound to Albumin: A significant portion of serum calcium is bound to albumin, but this bound form is inactive and does not directly contribute to physiological processes like nerve transmission and muscle contraction.

 

Educational Objective:


Ionized calcium is the biologically active form of calcium in the body and plays a crucial role in neuromuscular function, blood clotting, and bone metabolism. It is regulated by PTH, vitamin D, and calcitonin to maintain calcium homeostasis.

questions.stem: The force of muscle contraction can be increased by all except:

options.label: A
options.text: Increasing the frequency of activation of motor units.

options.label: B
options.text: Increasing the number of motor units activated.

options.label: C
options.text: Increasing the strength of stimuli from maximal to supramaximal.

options.label: D
options.text: Increasing the resting length of the muscle.

questions.answerText: Increasing the strength of stimuli from maximal to supramaximal.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Increasing the strength of stimuli from maximal to supramaximal.

 

The all-or-none law states that once a stimulus reaches the maximal level, increasing its strength further (to supramaximal) does not enhance force. The muscle fibers have already reached their peak contraction capacity. Supramaximal stimuli do not recruit additional motor units because all excitable fibers are already activated at the maximal stimulus. Instead, excessive stimulation can lead to tissue damage without additional functional benefit.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Increasing the frequency of activation of motor units: Higher stimulation frequency leads to summation and tetanus, increasing the force of contraction, as explained by Weber-Fechner’s Law.

 

Option B. Increasing the number of motor units activated: More motor units contracting leads to greater force production, following Henneman’s Size Principle, where smaller motor units activate first, followed by larger ones as force demand increases.

 

Option D. Increasing the resting length of the muscle: Within optimal physiological limits, increasing muscle length allows for maximum actin-myosin cross-bridge formation, enhancing force generation according to Frank-Starling Law.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Muscle contraction force can be increased by motor unit recruitment, higher activation frequency, and optimal muscle length. However, increasing stimulus beyond maximal does not further increase force due to the all-or-none law.

What is the approximate feedback "gain" of the arterial baroreceptors in this patient when they are functioning normally?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) -1.0

 

The feedback gain of a control system is calculated using the formula:

  • Correction is the difference between the change in blood pressure without baroreceptor function and with baroreceptor function.
  • Error Left is the difference between the final blood pressure with functional baroreceptors and the baseline pressure.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man was seen by neurologist because he had experienced prolonged episodes of tingling and numbness in his right arm. He underwent a neurologic exam to evaluate his sensory nervous system. Which of the following cutaneous mechanoreceptors is correctly paired with the type of stimulus to which it is most apt to respond?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Pacinian corpuscle and rapid vibration

 

Pacinian corpuscles are specialized mechanoreceptors located in the deep layers of the skin, including the dermis and subcutaneous tissue. They are most sensitive to rapid, high-frequency vibration (250–300 Hz) and deep pressure. These receptors quickly adapt to stimuli, making them crucial for detecting changes rather than sustained pressure.

 

  • Function: Pacinian corpuscles detect rapid vibrations, which help in sensing textures and vibrations through tools or surfaces (e.g., feeling vibrations through a steering wheel or detecting phone vibrations in a pocket).
  • Structure: They are encapsulated, lamellated receptors, allowing them to be highly responsive to mechanical changes but not sustained pressure.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Meissner corpuscle and skin stretch:

 

  • Meissner corpuscles are superficial mechanoreceptors responsible for light touch and two-point discrimination, but not skin stretch.
  • Ruffini endings, not Meissner corpuscles, detect skin stretch.

 

Option C. Merkel cells and slow vibration:

 

  • Merkel cells are responsible for fine touch and texture discrimination, not slow vibration.
  • They are crucial for reading Braille as they detect edges and points with high precision.

 

Option D. Ruffini corpuscles and sustained pressure:

 

  • Ruffini corpuscles are primarily responsible for skin stretch and joint angle proprioception, not sustained pressure.
  • Sustained pressure is better detected by Merkel cells and Pacinian corpuscles in certain conditions.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Pacinian corpuscles are rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors that respond to high-frequency vibrations and deep pressure, making them essential for detecting dynamic mechanical changes in the environment.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man loses his right hand in a farm accident. Four years later, he has episodes, of severe pain in the missing hand (phantom limb pain). A detailed PET scan study of his cerebral cortex might be expected to show:

options.label: A
options.text: Expansion of the right-hand area in his right primary somatosensory cortex.

options.label: B
options.text: Expansion of the right hand area in as left primary somatosensory cortex

options.label: C
options.text: Projection of fibers from neighbouring sensory areas into the right-hand area of his right primary somatosensory cortex.

options.label: D
options.text: Projection of fibers from neighbouring sensory areas into the right-hand area of his left primary somatosensory cortex.

questions.answerText: Projection of fibers from neighbouring sensory areas into the right-hand area of his left primary somatosensory cortex.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Projection of fibers from neighbouring sensory areas into the right-hand area of his left primary somatosensory cortex.

 

Phantom limb pain occurs due to cortical reorganization (neuroplasticity) following limb loss. The primary somatosensory cortex (S1), located in the postcentral gyrus, contains a somatotopic map (homunculus), where different body parts are represented contralaterally. Since the right hand is controlled by the left somatosensory cortex, after amputation, the unused cortical area starts receiving inputs from neighboring regions (such as the face or upper arm).

 

  • This phenomenon is known as cortical remapping and explains why some amputees feel sensations (including pain) in their missing limb when nearby areas (like the face) are touched.
  • The projection of sensory fibers into the deafferented hand area causes misinterpretation of stimuli, leading to phantom limb pain.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Expansion of the right-hand area in his right primary somatosensory cortex: The right primary somatosensory cortex does not process sensory input from the right hand, as sensory input is always contralateral.

 

Option B. Expansion of the right-hand area in his left primary somatosensory cortex: The lost hand’s cortical representation does not expand, but rather gets taken over by neighboring sensory areas, a process called cortical reorganization.

 

Option C. Projection of fibers from neighboring sensory areas into the right-hand area of his right primary somatosensory cortex: The right somatosensory cortex does not receive input from the right hand. The left somatosensory cortex is responsible for the right hand, making this answer incorrect.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Phantom limb pain occurs due to cortical remapping, where the neighboring sensory areas project into the deafferented cortical region. In this case, fibers from adjacent sensory areas (e.g., face or upper arm) project into the right-hand area of the left primary somatosensory cortex.

questions.stem: Polyphagia in diabetes is mainly due to:

options.label: A
options.text: Decreased glucose utilization in most of the tissues of the body

options.label: B
options.text: Decreased glucose uptake by whole brain

options.label: C
options.text: Decreased glucose utilization by entire hypothalamus nuclei

options.label: D
options.text: Decreased glucose utilization of VMH causing less VMI activity.

questions.answerText: Decreased glucose utilization of VMH causing less VMI activity.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Decreased glucose utilization of VMH causing less VMI activity.

 

Polyphagia (excessive hunger) in diabetes is due to the dysfunction of the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH), which is the satiety center of the brain. The VMH neurons require glucose for activation, and when glucose uptake is impaired (as seen in diabetes), the activity of these neurons decreases, leading to persistent hunger.

 

  • The ventromedial hypothalamic nucleus (VMH) plays a key role in regulating food intake by inhibiting hunger when glucose levels are adequate.
  • In diabetes, due to insulin resistance or deficiency, glucose is not efficiently utilized by VMH neurons, leading to reduced inhibitory signals, making the body feel constantly hungry.
  • This lack of satiety contributes to polyphagia, one of the three classic symptoms of diabetes (polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Decreased glucose utilization in most of the tissues of the body: While diabetes causes decreased glucose utilization in peripheral tissues (e.g., muscle and adipose tissue), this leads to hyperglycemia, but not necessarily polyphagia.

 

Option B. Decreased glucose uptake by the whole brain: The brain does not depend on insulin for glucose uptake; it uses GLUT-1 and GLUT-3 transporters, which are insulin-independent. Only VMH dysfunction specifically contributes to increased hunger.

 

Option C. Decreased glucose utilization by the entire hypothalamic nuclei: Not all hypothalamic nuclei regulate hunger; only the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) is responsible for satiety control.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Polyphagia in diabetes is caused by decreased glucose utilization in the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH), leading to reduced satiety signals. This is due to impaired insulin-dependent glucose uptake, which results in the brain perceiving a state of starvation despite high blood glucose levels.

questions.stem: Which of the following hormone is reported to promote maturation of hypothalamic gonadal axis during puberty?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Leptin

 

Leptin, a hormone primarily secreted by adipose tissue, plays a crucial role in initiating and regulating puberty by acting on the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis.

 

  • During childhood, as body fat increases, leptin levels rise.
  • Leptin signals the hypothalamus that the body has adequate energy reserves to support reproductive function.
  • It stimulates the release of Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH) from the hypothalamus, which in turn promotes Luteinizing Hormone (LH) and Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH) release from the pituitary, leading to puberty.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Insulin: While insulin influences metabolism and growth, it does not directly regulate the maturation of the hypothalamic-gonadal axis.

 

Option B. Testosterone: Testosterone is a key hormone during puberty, but it is an effector hormone rather than a regulator of puberty onset. It is produced after the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis is activated.

 

Option D. Luteinizing Hormone (LH): LH is critical for testosterone and estrogen production but is released after GnRH stimulation. The question asks for a hormone that promotes maturation of the HPG axis, which is leptin, not LH.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Leptin, secreted by adipose tissue, plays a key role in triggering puberty by stimulating GnRH release, thereby promoting the maturation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis.

options.label: B

options.label: C

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Compliance is slightly greater when measured during deflation than when measured during inflation

 

Pulmonary compliance refers to the lung’s ability to expand and stretch in response to pressure changes. It is defined as:

Hysteresis and Compliance Curve:

 

  • Lung compliance is not the same during inflation and deflation due to a phenomenon called hysteresis, observed in the pressure-volume compliance curve.
  • During deflation (expiration), compliance is slightly higher than during inflation because surfactant molecules are better aligned to reduce alveolar surface tension, making lung expansion easier.
  • This explains why compliance is greater when measured during deflation than during inflation.

 

Other Options:

questions.stem: In regional ventilation and perfusion of the lung, which of the following is correct:

options.label: A
options.text: Upper regions of the lung ventilate better than the lower regions

options.label: B
options.text: When supine the apical and basal ventilation is equal

options.label: C
options.text: V/Q ratio increases down the lung

options.label: D
options.text: The highest alveolar PO2, is at the base of the lung.

questions.answerText: When supine the apical and basal ventilation is equal
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) When supine the apical and basal ventilation is equal

 

Lung ventilation and perfusion vary due to gravity, which affects both in an upright posture but changes in a supine position.

 

  • In an upright posture:
    • The apex (upper lung) has lower ventilation and much lower perfusion, making the V/Q ratio high.
    • The base (lower lung) has higher ventilation but even greater perfusion, leading to a lower V/Q ratio.
  • When supine:
    • The effect of gravity is nullified, leading to equal ventilation per unit area between the apical and basal lung regions.

 

This is why option B is correct—in the supine position, per unit area, ventilation at the apex and base becomes similar.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Upper regions of the lung ventilate better than the lower regions: Ventilation is actually higher at the base in the upright position due to increased lung compliance and gravitational effects.

 

Option C. V/Q ratio increases down the lung:

 

  • V/Q ratio actually decreases as you move from the apex to the base.
  • This is because perfusion increases more than ventilation as you go downward.

 

Option D. The highest alveolar PO₂ is at the base of the lung:

 

  • Alveolar PO₂ is highest at the apex, not at the base, because V/Q ratio is highest at the apex, leading to better oxygenation relative to blood flow.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In the supine position, the effect of gravity on ventilation distribution is minimized, leading to equal ventilation per unit area at both the apex and the base of the lung.

questions.stem: Which one of the following definitions is incorrect?

options.label: A
options.text: The respiratory minute volume equals the amount of air inspired per minute.

options.label: B
options.text: Residual volume is the air left in the lungs after a maximal expiratory effort

options.label: C
options.text: Vital capacity is the maximal amount of air that can be expired after a normal inspiration

options.label: D
options.text: Physiological dead space is the amount of air not equilibrating with blood.

questions.answerText: Vital capacity is the maximal amount of air that can be expired after a normal inspiration
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Vital capacity is the maximal amount of air that can be expired after a normal inspiration.

 

Vital capacity (VC) is the maximum amount of air that can be exhaled after a forceful inspiration, not after a normal inspiration. It includes:

 

  • Tidal volume (TV) – Normal breathing volume
  • Inspiratory reserve volume (IRV) – Additional air that can be inhaled after normal inspiration
  • Expiratory reserve volume (ERV) – Additional air that can be exhaled after normal expiration

 

Thus, VC = TV + IRV + ERV. The incorrect part of the statement is "after a normal inspiration" instead of "after a forceful inspiration".

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. The respiratory minute volume equals the amount of air inspired per minute:

 

  • This is correct. Minute ventilation (or respiratory minute volume) is calculated as: Minute Ventilation = Tidal Volume × Respiratory Rate
  • It represents the total volume of air moved in and out of the lungs per minute.

 

Option B. Residual volume is the air left in the lungs after a maximal expiratory effort: This is correct. Residual volume (RV) is the amount of air remaining in the lungs after maximal exhalation, preventing lung collapse.

 

Option D. Physiological dead space is the amount of air not equilibrating with blood:

 

  • This is correct. Physiological dead space consists of:
    • Anatomical dead space (airways where no gas exchange occurs, such as the trachea and bronchi).
    • Alveolar dead space (alveoli that are ventilated but not perfused, meaning no gas exchange occurs).
  • Since this air does not equilibrate with blood, the definition is correct.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Vital capacity (VC) is the maximum volume of air exhaled after a forceful inspiration. The incorrect definition stated that it is after a normal inspiration, which is not true.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old male presents to emergency with severe sudden-onset heart palpitations. The patient reports symptoms of chest pain, fatigue, and dizziness. Upon examination, his heart rate is 165/min and regular. His blood pressure is 106/74 mmHg. A gentle massage below the level of the left mandible elicits an immediate improvement in the patient, as his heart rate returns to 60/min. What was the mechanism of action of this manoeuvre?

options.label: A
options.text: Increasing the refractory period in ventricular myocytes

options.label: B
options.text: Increasing sympathetic tone in systemic arteries

options.label: C
options.text: Decreasing the firing rate of carotid baroreceptors

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Slowing conduction in AV node

 

The patient likely had paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT), a condition often involving reentrant circuits through the AV node. Carotid massage is a well-known vagal maneuver that stimulates baroreceptors in the carotid sinus, leading to an increase in parasympathetic (vagal) activity and a decrease in sympathetic tone.

 

  • Mechanism of Carotid Massage:
  1. Stimulates carotid sinus baroreceptors → sends signals via the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) to the brainstem.
  2. Brainstem increases parasympathetic (vagal) output → via the vagus nerve (CN X).
  3. Vagus nerve acts on the AV node → slows AV nodal conduction by decreasing the slope of phase 4 depolarization in pacemaker cells.
  4. Interrupts reentrant circuits in AV nodal-dependent tachycardias (e.g., PSVT), restoring normal sinus rhythm.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Increasing the refractory period in ventricular myocytes: Carotid massage primarily affects the AV node, not the ventricles. Ventricular myocytes are not directly influenced by vagal stimulation.

 

Option B. Increasing sympathetic tone in systemic arteries: Carotid massage actually leads to decreased sympathetic tone, causing vasodilation and reduced heart rate, not increased sympathetic tone.

 

Option C. Decreasing the firing rate of carotid baroreceptors: Carotid massage increases the firing of carotid baroreceptors, leading to reflex parasympathetic activation and sympathetic inhibition.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Carotid massage stimulates baroreceptors, which increases vagal tone, leading to slowed AV nodal conduction. This is useful in terminating AV nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT) and restoring normal sinus rhythm.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male presents to the physician with significantly enlarged thyroid gland. Serum T3/T4 levels are decreased. lodine deficiency is suspected. Which of the following is the function of thyroid peroxidase in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Oxidation of iodide

 

Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) is an enzyme located in the apical membrane of thyroid follicular cells and plays a key role in thyroid hormone synthesis. It catalyzes three major reactions:

 

  1. Oxidation of iodide (I⁻ to I₂): TPO converts iodide (I⁻) into its active form, iodine (I₂), which is necessary for thyroid hormone synthesis.
  2. Iodination of tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin: This forms monoiodotyrosine (MIT) and diiodotyrosine (DIT).
  3. Coupling of iodotyrosines: TPO facilitates the coupling of MIT and DIT to form T3 (triiodothyronine) and T4 (thyroxine).

 

Thus, the correct function of TPO in this patient is the oxidation of iodide to prepare it for incorporation into thyroid hormones.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Na⁺-Iodide uptake: Incorrect, as iodine uptake into the thyroid follicular cells occurs via the sodium-iodide symporter (NIS), not TPO.

 

Option C. Thyroglobulin synthesis: Incorrect, because thyroglobulin is synthesized in the follicular cells and transported into the colloid. This process is mediated by ribosomes and the Golgi apparatus, not TPO.

 

Option D. Iodotyrosine deiodination: Incorrect, as deiodination is carried out by deiodinases (D1, D2, D3), not TPO. These enzymes help recycle iodine from MIT and DIT.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) catalyzes the oxidation of iodide (I⁻ to I₂), iodination of tyrosine residues, and coupling of iodotyrosines in thyroid hormone synthesis.

questions.stem: A healthy, 25-year-old medical student participates in a 20-kilometer charity run for the Indian Medical Association. Which muscles does the student use (contract) during expiration while running?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Internal intercostals and abdominal recti

 

During normal (quiet) expiration, exhalation is a passive process due to lung elastic recoil, and no active muscular contraction is needed. However, during exercise or forced expiration, additional muscles are recruited to actively expel air from the lungs.

 

  1. Internal intercostals: Pull the ribs downward and inward, reducing thoracic volume.
  2. Abdominal muscles (rectus abdominis, external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis): Contract to increase intra-abdominal pressure, pushing the diaphragm upward, which helps force air out.

 

This active expiration helps in efficient ventilation during intense physical activity such as running.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Diaphragm and external intercostals: These muscles are inspiratory muscles. The diaphragm contracts during inspiration, not expiration. External intercostals also assist in inspiration by elevating the ribs.

 

Option B. Diaphragm and internal intercostals: The diaphragm does not participate in expiration, only in inspiration. While internal intercostals do assist in forced expiration, the abdominal muscles play a key role, which is missing in this option.

 

 

Option D. Sternocleidomastoid muscles: Sternocleidomastoids are accessory muscles of inspiration, not expiration. They help lift the sternum and expand the thoracic cavity during deep breathing.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Forced expiration during exercise is an active process that involves internal intercostals and abdominal muscles, which work together to expel air forcefully from the lungs.

questions.stemHtml: While analyzing the impact of acute blood loss on cardiac function by interpreting changes in the Frank Starling curves. Understanding how various clinical interventions or pathophysiological states affect stroke volume is vital. Given the patient's condition of mild hemorrhage and the associated compensatory mechanisms, to which point will the stroke volume shift from point X on the graph?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Point A

 

The question presents a scenario of mild hemorrhage and asks about the resulting shift on a Frank-Starling curve from point X.

Mild hemorrhage leads to a decrease in blood volume, which reduces venous return, causing a fall in central venous pressure and cardiac output—moving the heart to a lower position on the curve (as indicated by point X on the graph).

 

However, the body responds through compensatory mechanisms, primarily via the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS). Activation of RAAS leads to:

 

  • ↑ Angiotensin II (Ag II) production
  • ↑ Venoconstriction, which increases venous return
  • Restoration of central venous pressure and stroke volume

 

With these compensations, the heart can move back along the same Starling curve, improving cardiac output slightly. However, since this is a mild hemorrhage and not a severe one, the full recovery to the previous higher curve is not expected.

 

Thus, the expected shift is from point X to point A—on the same curve, but with improved venous return and cardiac output compared to point X.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Point C: This point lies on a higher Starling curve, representing enhanced contractility or increased inotropy, which is not the expected compensatory response to mild hemorrhage. There’s no indication of increased inotropy—only volume restoration via RAAS and venoconstriction. Therefore, movement to point C is incorrect.

 

Option C. Point B: Point B also lies on a higher curve and indicates increased stroke volume and cardiac output, more than would be restored by venoconstriction alone. Since the body isn’t increasing contractility directly in mild hemorrhage, point B is not accurate.

 

Option D. Point E: Point E represents a further decline from point X—indicating worsening shock or uncompensated hemorrhage, which contradicts the presence of compensatory mechanisms (e.g., RAAS, venoconstriction). Hence, this is also incorrect.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Mild hemorrhage activates RAAS, increasing angiotensin II and venoconstriction, which improves venous return and shifts the Frank-Starling position along the same curve, increasing cardiac output.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy presents with progressive muscle weakness and difficulty walking. He was recently diagnosed with poliomyelitis, which has affected his motor neurons. Upon investigation, a biopsy of his nerve cells reveals impaired axonal transport. Which of the following pairs correctly identifies the motor proteins involved in anterograde and retrograde axonal transport, respectively, in the affected neurons?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Kinesin and dynein

 

Neurons rely on axonal transport to move essential materials between the cell body (soma) and the axon terminals. This process is mediated by two major motor proteins:

 

  1. Kinesin (Anterograde Transport) → Moves cargo away from the cell body (soma to axon terminal)
    • Transports vesicles, mitochondria, neurotransmitters, and organelles towards the synaptic terminal.
    • Requires ATP and moves along microtubules towards the (+)-end (anterograde).
  2. Dynein (Retrograde Transport) → Moves cargo towards the cell body (axon terminal to soma)
    • Transports recycled vesicles, growth factors, and harmful substances (e.g., viruses and toxins) back to the soma.
    • Moves along microtubules towards the (-)-end (retrograde).

 

Clinical Relevance:

 

  • Poliomyelitis, herpes, rabies, and tetanus toxin use retrograde transport (dynein) to travel from peripheral nerves to the CNS, leading to infection.
  • Damage to kinesin-mediated transport impairs neurotransmitter delivery, affecting synaptic function and muscle control, seen in motor neuron diseases.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. SNARE and Calmodulin:

 

  • SNARE proteins are involved in vesicle docking and neurotransmitter release, not axonal transport.
  • Calmodulin is a calcium-binding protein involved in signaling, not transport.

 

Option B. Dynein and Kinesin: The order is incorrect. Dynein is for retrograde, and kinesin is for anterograde transport.

 

Option C. Calmodulin and SNARE: Neither of these proteins are involved in axonal transport.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Kinesin mediates anterograde transport (soma → axon terminal) to deliver essential cellular components.
  • Dynein mediates retrograde transport (axon terminal → soma) to recycle materials and transport pathogens like polio, rabies, and tetanus toxin back to the CNS.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the incorrect match?

options.label: A
options.text: Gastrin from G cells from stomach

options.label: B
options.text: GIP from L cells from duodenum and jejunum

options.label: C
options.text: Secretin from S cells of duodenum and jejunum

options.label: D
options.text: CCK from I cell of duodenum and pancreas

questions.answerText: GIP from L cells from duodenum and jejunum
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) GIP from L cells from duodenum and jejunum

 

  • GIP (Glucose-dependent Insulinotropic Peptide) → K cells of the duodenum and jejunum (Incorrect)
    • Stimulates insulin release in response to glucose (incretin effect) and inhibits gastric acid secretion.
    • L cells secrete GLP-1 (Glucagon-like Peptide-1), NOT GIP.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Gastrin from G cells of the stomach: Correct

 

  • This match is accurate.
  • G cells, located in the stomach, secrete gastrin, a hormone that stimulates gastric acid secretion.

 

Option C. Secretin from S cells of the duodenum and jejunum: Correct

 

  • This is also a correct match.
  • S cells, found in the duodenum and jejunum, secrete secretin.
  • Secretin is involved in regulating the pH of the small intestine by promoting the release of bicarbonate from the pancreas.

 

Option D. CCK from I cells of the duodenum and pancreas: Partially incorrect (I cells are found in the duodenum and jejunum, but not in the pancreas).

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • GIP is secreted by K cells (not L cells) and stimulates insulin release.
  • L cells secrete GLP-1, an incretin hormone that enhances insulin secretion.
  • I cells release CCK, which promotes gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme secretion but are not found in the pancreas.

questions.stem: The tact lie discrimination will be affected in the lesion of this ascending sensory pathway of the spinal cord?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Posterior column

 

Tactile (or two-point) discrimination refers to the ability to distinguish between two closely spaced stimuli on the skin. This function is mediated by the Dorsal (Posterior) Column-Medial Lemniscus (DCML) pathway, which carries fine touch, proprioception, and vibration sensation.

 

  • The Posterior Column-Medial Lemniscus Pathway includes:
    • Fasciculus gracilis (lower limb and trunk)
    • Fasciculus cuneatus (upper limb and trunk)
  • This pathway transmits sensory information to the medulla, then crosses over (decussates) to the contralateral medial lemniscus, traveling to the thalamus and somatosensory cortex.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Spinothalamic tract: Transmits pain, temperature, and crude touch, not fine touch or discrimination.

 

Option C. Spinoreticular tract: Involved in autonomic and emotional responses to pain, not tactile discrimination.

 

Option D. Lateral lemniscus: Part of the auditory pathway, unrelated to tactile sensation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Tactile (two-point) discrimination is mediated by the Posterior Column-Medial Lemniscus Pathway, which is responsible for fine touch, proprioception, and vibration. Lesions in this pathway impair sensory discrimination and proprioception.
