questions.stem: In the cardiac muscle, the inhibition of Na+ K+ ATPase results in?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Depolarisation

 

The Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump plays a crucial role in maintaining the resting membrane potential (RMP) by actively transporting 3 Na⁺ out of the cell and 2 K⁺ in, contributing to negative intracellular potential.

 

  • When the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase is inhibited, Na⁺ accumulates inside the cardiac muscle cell, while K⁺ efflux is reduced.
  • This leads to less negativity inside the cell (membrane potential becomes less negative), causing depolarization.
  • Since Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase contributes to about 5-10% of RMP, its inhibition makes the cell more excitable and can increase intracellular Ca²⁺ levels indirectly (by affecting Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger), potentially enhancing cardiac contractility (a mechanism exploited by cardiac glycosides like digoxin).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hyperpolarization and then depolarization: Not correct because Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase inhibition leads directly to depolarization, without an initial hyperpolarization.

 

Option C. Hyperpolarization: because inhibition of Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase prevents the usual outward Na⁺ movement, making the inside of the cell more positive (depolarized) rather than hyperpolarized.

 

Option D. Repolarization: Repolarization involves K⁺ efflux through different channels, and Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase inhibition does not promote repolarization but rather prevents full repolarization.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Inhibition of Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase in cardiac muscle results in depolarization due to accumulation of intracellular Na⁺ and reduced K⁺ influx, leading to increased excitability of the cardiac cells.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old male had headache, palpitations and difficulty in breathing during his mountain trekking (climbing). His SPO2 was found to be decreased (<80%) leading to clinical features of acute mountain sickness. Which of the following nerve fibers are most susceptible to these hypoxic changes?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) B fibers

 

  • B fibers are preganglionic autonomic fibers, which play a role in autonomic regulation of blood pressure, respiration, and heart rate.
  • Hypoxia in high-altitude environments primarily affects autonomic regulation, leading to symptoms like tachycardia, dyspnea, and altered vasomotor control.
  • This makes B fibers the most susceptible to hypoxic injury in AMS.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. A fibers: Less affected due to larger diameter and myelination.

 

Option C. C fibers: Least affected as they are unmyelinated and slow-conducting.

 

Option D. D fibers: Not a recognized category in standard nerve fiber classification.

 

Educational Objective:

 

B fibers (small myelinated autonomic fibers) are the most susceptible to hypoxia and are affected in conditions like acute mountain sickness, leading to autonomic dysfunction such as tachycardia, dyspnea, and vascular instability.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following does this graph signify?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Bronchitis 

 

The given graph represents a spirometry test, showing the Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 second (FEV₁) and Forced Vital Capacity (FVC) ratio, which is crucial in distinguishing obstructive from restrictive lung diseases.

 

  • FEV₁/FVC = 47% (Reduced)
  • Normal FEV₁/FVC = 75-85%

 

A FEV₁/FVC ratio below 70% strongly indicates an obstructive lung disease like chronic bronchitis, emphysema, or asthma.

 

  • In obstructive lung diseases, airway resistance increases, leading to decreased FEV₁ (difficulty in expelling air).
  • Chronic bronchitis, a type of COPD, is characterized by mucus hypersecretion, inflammation, and airway narrowing, leading to low FEV₁/FVC ratio.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Normal lung function: As normal FEV₁/FVC is 75-85%, and the given graph shows a significantly reduced value (47%), indicating obstruction.

 

Option C. Fibrosis (Restrictive Lung Disease): Because restrictive lung diseases (e.g., pulmonary fibrosis) have a normal or increased FEV₁/FVC ratio (>80%), due to proportional reduction in both FEV₁ and FVC.

 

Option D. Both B and C: As only bronchitis (obstructive disease) is indicated, not fibrosis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • FEV₁/FVC <70% suggests an obstructive lung disease (e.g., bronchitis, emphysema, asthma).
  • FEV₁/FVC ≥80% suggests a restrictive lung disease (e.g., fibrosis, interstitial lung disease).
  • This graph strongly suggests chronic bronchitis, a type of COPD, due to the severely reduced FEV₁/FVC ratio (47%).

questions.stem: A 30-year-old mountaineer presents to the clinic after returning from a high-altitude expedition. He reports experiencing fatigue and shortness of breath while at high altitudes. Which of the following is least likely to be observed in this individual as a physiological adaptation to high altitude?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Hypoventilation

 

At high altitude, the partial pressure of oxygen (PO₂) decreases, leading to hypoxia. The body undergoes several physiological adaptations to increase oxygen delivery to tissues and compensate for the reduced oxygen availability:

 

  1. Hyperventilation occurs, not hypoventilation – The low oxygen levels at high altitude stimulate the peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid bodies), which signal the respiratory center in the medulla to increase breathing rate (hyperventilation).
  2. Hyperventilation increases oxygen intake but also leads to hypocapnia (low CO₂ levels), which can result in respiratory alkalosis.
  3. Hypoventilation does not occur because it would further decrease oxygen levels, worsening hypoxia.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Polycythemia:

 

  • Hypoxia stimulates erythropoietin (EPO) release, primarily from the kidneys (~80%) and liver (~15%), leading to increased red blood cell (RBC) production.
  • This helps increase oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood.

 

Option B. Increase in Hb: Along with polycythemia, hemoglobin synthesis increases to improve oxygen transport and delivery to tissues.

 

Option C. Increase in Myoglobin: Myoglobin, an oxygen-binding protein in skeletal and cardiac muscles, increases to store more oxygen for muscle activity, ensuring adequate supply during low oxygen availability.

 

Educational Objective:

 

At high altitude, the body compensates for hypoxia by hyperventilation, polycythemia, increased hemoglobin levels, and higher myoglobin concentrations. Hypoventilation is least likely, as it would worsen oxygen deprivation rather than improving it.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the hormones A & B giving negative feedback on Hypothalamus - Pituitary axis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Inhibin & Testosterone 

 

The Hypothalamus-Pituitary-Gonadal (HPG) axis is regulated by negative feedback mechanisms to maintain hormonal balance.

 

  1. Testosterone (B) – Released by Leydig cells in the testes. It exerts negative feedback on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, suppressing the release of:
    • Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH) from the hypothalamus.
    • Luteinizing Hormone (LH) from the anterior pituitary, which stimulates testosterone production.
  2. Inhibin (A) – Released by Sertoli cells in the testes. It selectively inhibits Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH) release from the anterior pituitary, reducing spermatogenesis when sperm production is sufficient.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Testosterone & Inhibin: Correct pair, but the order should be Inhibin & Testosterone.

 

Option B. Estrogen & Progesterone: These are female hormones that regulate the female reproductive axis.

 

Option D. Testosterone & Progesterone: Progesterone is not a significant inhibitor in the male HPG axis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In the male Hypothalamus-Pituitary-Gonadal (HPG) axis), Testosterone (from Leydig cells) inhibits GnRH and LH, while Inhibin (from Sertoli cells) inhibits FSH to regulate spermatogenesis and hormonal balance.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with symptoms of severe hypertension and is suspected to have a renal origin for her condition. Imaging studies and kidney biopsy reveal abnormalities localized to the medulla of the kidney. Which of the following structures is least likely to be involved, given its primary location is outside the medulla?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Juxtaglomerular apparatus

 

The Juxtaglomerular Apparatus (JGA) is located in the renal cortex, near the glomerulus, where the afferent arteriole meets the distal tubule. Since the pathology in this patient is localized to the medulla, the JGA is the least likely structure to be involved because it is not present in the medulla. It plays a crucial role in renin secretion and blood pressure regulation, but it does not extend into the medulla.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Loop of Henle: Located in the medulla, where it plays a key role in urine concentration through the countercurrent multiplier system.

 

Option B. Vasa recta: A network of capillaries found in the renal medulla, responsible for countercurrent exchange, helping maintain the osmotic gradient.

 

Option C. Collecting duct: Extends from the cortex to the medulla, where it regulates final urine concentration under the influence of antidiuretic hormone (ADH).

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Juxtaglomerular Apparatus (JGA) is located in the renal cortex and is responsible for renin secretion and blood pressure regulation.

questions.stemHtml: The rate of diffusion of a substance is plotted against concentration gradient in the following graph. The substance is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Glucose

 

The given graph represents the relationship between the rate of diffusion and the concentration gradient. The characteristic shape of the curve suggests that the process is carrier-mediated transport, as the rate of diffusion increases rapidly at first but then reaches a maximum saturation level (Vmax). This is because carrier proteins become fully occupied, preventing any further increase in diffusion rate beyond this point.

 

Glucose transport in cells occurs through facilitated diffusion, which is mediated by GLUT (Glucose Transporter) proteins. Unlike simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion relies on these transporters, which eventually become saturated when all binding sites are occupied. This saturation effect explains the plateau observed in the graph.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. CO₂: Carbon dioxide diffuses through the cell membrane via simple diffusion, which does not show saturation. The rate of simple diffusion continues to increase linearly with an increasing concentration gradient, unlike the curve shown in the graph.

 

Option B. Na⁺: Sodium ions typically require active transport (e.g., via sodium-potassium pumps) or ion channels, which operate differently from facilitated diffusion. While some ion channels may become saturated, their transport kinetics often differ from glucose carriers.

 

Option D. Tri-iodothyronine: This hormone (T₃) is lipid-soluble and diffuses freely through the plasma membrane without the need for transporters. Since simple diffusion does not exhibit saturation, this substance does not match the graph.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Facilitated diffusion of glucose occurs via carrier proteins (GLUT transporters) and follows saturation kinetics, unlike simple diffusion.

questions.stemHtml: In the following LV pressure-volume loop diagram, point C denotes:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Aortic valve opens

 

The Left Ventricular (LV) Pressure-Volume Loop is a key concept in cardiovascular physiology, representing the different phases of the cardiac cycle.

 

  • Point C on the diagram represents the moment when the aortic valve closes. This occurs at the end of ventricular systole, when the left ventricle has ejected blood into the aorta, and the pressure in the ventricle starts to fall. The closure of the aortic valve marks the beginning of isovolumetric relaxation, where the left ventricle relaxes without any change in volume.
  • This event is crucial in preventing blood from flowing back into the left ventricle from the aorta. The second heart sound (S2) is also associated with the closing of the aortic and pulmonary valves.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Mitral valve closes: The mitral valve closes at Point A, which marks the beginning of isovolumetric contraction (MAMCOCO: Mitral valve closes → Aortic valve opens → Aortic valve closes → Mitral valve opens).

 

Option B. Aortic valve opens: The aortic valve opens at Point B, when ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure, allowing blood to be ejected into the aorta.

 

Option D. Mitral valve opens: The mitral valve opens at Point D, marking the start of ventricular filling when the ventricle relaxes and blood flows from the left atrium into the left ventricle.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The aortic valve closes at the end of ventricular systole, marking the start of isovolumetric relaxation in the left ventricle.

questions.stemHtml: One transport system across the cell membrane is given below. The process indicates which of the following:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Simple diffusion

 

The given image represents a lipid bilayer with molecules moving from a region of higher concentration to lower concentration, without the involvement of any carrier or channel protein. This indicates simple diffusion, a passive transport process that relies on the natural movement of molecules down their concentration gradient.

 

Key characteristics of simple diffusion:

 

  • No requirement for carrier proteins or membrane channels.
  • Movement occurs passively, without the need for ATP.
  • Common for small, non-polar molecules like oxygen (O₂), carbon dioxide (CO₂), and lipid-soluble molecules.

 

Since the diagram does not show specific transporters or channels, it confirms that the process depicted is simple diffusion.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Facilitated diffusion: Facilitated diffusion also occurs along a concentration gradient, but it requires carrier or channel proteins to transport substances across the membrane, which are not present in the given image.

 

Option C. Primary active transport: Active transport moves molecules against the concentration gradient (low to high) and requires ATP-dependent transport proteins, which are absent in the diagram.

 

Option D. Secondary active transport: This mechanism uses energy from an existing ion gradient (e.g., Na⁺ gradient) to transport molecules, often involving symporters or antiporters. No such system is depicted in the image.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Simple diffusion is a passive transport mechanism in which molecules move from a high concentration to a low concentration across the cell membrane without the need for carrier proteins or ATP.

questions.stem: MRI of the brain shows a lesion in the left precentral gyrus. Damage to which of the following functions is most likely responsible for his symptoms?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Voluntary movement

 

The precentral gyrus is located in the frontal lobe of the brain and forms the primary motor cortex (Brodmann area 4). This area is primarily responsible for initiating voluntary movements by sending motor signals to different parts of the body via the corticospinal tract.

 

  • A lesion in the left precentral gyrus would cause motor deficits (weakness or paralysis) on the right side of the body due to the contralateral control of movement by the motor cortex.
  • This is different from the postcentral gyrus, which is located in the parietal lobe and is associated with sensory processing.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Vision: Vision is primarily processed by the occipital lobe (visual cortex, Brodmann areas 17, 18, 19), which is not affected in this case. The precentral gyrus has no direct role in vision.

 

Option B. Olfaction: The olfactory system is primarily controlled by the olfactory bulb, olfactory tract, and piriform cortex in the temporal lobe. The precentral gyrus does not play a role in the sense of smell.

 

Option C. Auditory identification: Auditory processing, including speech and sound recognition, occurs in the temporal lobe (superior temporal gyrus, Wernicke's area, and auditory cortex). The precentral gyrus is unrelated to auditory function.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The precentral gyrus (primary motor cortex) is responsible for voluntary movement. Damage to this area leads to motor deficits, typically on the contralateral side of the body.

questions.stemHtml: The following diagram is from adrenal gland. Hormone produced by the marked area A in the following image is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Aldosterone 

 

The adrenal gland is divided into two main parts: the cortex and the medulla. The cortex has three distinct zones, which can be remembered using the mnemonic "GFR" (Zona Glomerulosa, Zona Fasciculata, Zona Reticularis).

 

  • A (Zona Glomerulosa): This outermost layer of the adrenal cortex is responsible for the production of mineralocorticoids, primarily aldosterone. Aldosterone plays a crucial role in sodium retention and potassium excretion, helping regulate blood pressure and electrolyte balance.
  • B (Zona Fasciculata): This middle layer produces glucocorticoids, mainly cortisol, which is involved in metabolism, immune response, and stress adaptation.
  • C (Zona Reticularis): This innermost layer produces androgens such as dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), which can be converted into testosterone and estrogen.

 

The adrenal medulla (not marked in this diagram) produces catecholamines like epinephrine and norepinephrine, which are involved in the fight-or-flight response.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Cortisol: Cortisol is produced by the zona fasciculata (B), not the zona glomerulosa.

 

Option C. Epinephrine: Epinephrine is secreted by the adrenal medulla, not the cortex.

 

Option D. Androgen: Androgens are produced by the zona reticularis (C), not the zona glomerulosa.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex produces aldosterone, a mineralocorticoid that regulates sodium and potassium balance, contributing to blood pressure control.

questions.stemHtml: In the following diagram, the curve "X" represents the normal relationship of alveolar ventilation with PaCO2, when PaO2 is 100mmHg. If pH changed from 7.4 to 7.3, change in alveolar ventilation will shift to which of the curve?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Curve C 

Points to be understood from this graph: 

 

The graph represents the relationship between alveolar ventilation (L/min) and alveolar PCO₂ (mmHg) under different physiological conditions.

 

  • Curve "X" is the normal curve, where PaO₂ = 100 mmHg and pH = 7.4.
  • A decrease in pH (from 7.4 to 7.3) represents respiratory acidosis or metabolic acidosis, which stimulates the central chemoreceptors in the medulla.
  • This leads to an increase in alveolar ventilation to compensate for the acidosis by removing excess CO₂ through hyperventilation.

 

Since ventilation must increase, the new curve should be shifted leftward and upward compared to the normal curve (X). Curve D represents this shift, as it is parallel to X but at a higher level of ventilation for the same PaCO₂.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Curve B: Curve B is positioned too far to the right, indicating a state of hypoventilation, which does not match the condition of acidosis-induced hyperventilation.

 

Option B. Curve C: Curve C is too low, meaning it represents a lower ventilatory response than what would be expected for a pH drop to 7.3.

 

Option D. Curve E: Curve E is too extreme, suggesting a greater ventilatory response than would occur with just a 0.1 pH drop.

 

Educational Objective:

 

A decrease in pH (acidosis) leads to an increase in alveolar ventilation to remove CO₂. The ventilatory response shifts to a curve that is parallel to the normal but at a higher ventilation rate, which in this case is represented by Curve D.

questions.stem: Best index for afterload?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) MAP

 

Afterload refers to the resistance the left ventricle must overcome to eject blood into the systemic circulation. It is primarily determined by arterial pressure and vascular resistance.

 

  • MAP (Mean Arterial Pressure) is the best measurable index of afterload because it directly represents the average pressure in the arteries during one cardiac cycle, which the heart must pump against.
  • Higher MAP = Higher Afterload, meaning the heart must work harder to push blood forward.

 

Although TPR (Total Peripheral Resistance) influences afterload, it is not directly measurable in clinical settings, whereas MAP is a practical and direct measure of afterload.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. End Diastolic Volume (EDV): EDV is a measure of preload, not afterload. It represents the volume of blood in the left ventricle before contraction.

 

Option C. End Systolic Volume (ESV): ESV refers to the amount of blood left in the ventricle after systole. While it is influenced by afterload, it is not the best index for it.

 

Option D. Total Peripheral Resistance (TPR): TPR is a determinant of afterload rather than an index. Higher TPR increases afterload, but it is not a directly measurable index like MAP.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) is the best index for afterload because it represents the pressure the heart must overcome to eject blood. Total Peripheral Resistance (TPR) determines afterload but is not directly measurable in clinical practice.

questions.stem: Human genome has max genes for which of the following:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Odorant receptors

 

Among the various gene families present in the human genome, the odorant receptor (OR) gene family has the largest number of genes.

 

  • Odorant receptors (ORs) are responsible for detecting a vast range of smells.
  • The human genome contains ~1000 genes related to olfaction, making it the largest gene family.
  • These genes encode G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs), which are located in the olfactory epithelium.
  • Even though humans have a large number of olfactory receptor genes, many are non-functional (pseudogenes), reducing our sense of smell compared to animals like dogs or rodents, which have a much higher number of functional odorant receptor genes.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Immunoglobulin: The genes coding for immunoglobulins (antibodies) undergo recombination to generate diversity, but their absolute number in the genome is much lower than that of odorant receptors.

 

Option B. Growth Factor: Growth factors such as EGF, FGF, and IGF have relatively fewer genes compared to odorant receptors. They play essential roles in cell growth, differentiation, and repair, but they do not form the largest gene family.

 

Option C. Interleukin: 

 

  • Interleukins (ILs) are signaling molecules that regulate immune responses, and their gene family is much smaller compared to odorant receptor genes.
  • The number of interleukin genes in humans is much less than 100, making it significantly smaller than the odorant receptor gene family.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Odorant receptor genes form the largest gene family in the human genome, with approximately 1000 genes dedicated to detecting and distinguishing different smells.

questions.stem: Anatomical dead space is measured with:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Single breath nitrogen test 

 

Anatomical dead space refers to the volume of air in the respiratory passages (nose, trachea, bronchi) that does not participate in gas exchange. It is measured using the Single Breath Nitrogen Test (Fowler’s Method).

 

  • This test involves a single deep breath of pure oxygen, followed by a gradual exhalation while nitrogen concentration is continuously measured.
  • The nitrogen washout curve helps determine the transition point between dead space and alveolar air, thereby quantifying anatomical dead space.
  • The principle behind this is that the first part of exhaled air comes from the dead space, which contains little nitrogen, followed by alveolar air, which has a higher nitrogen concentration.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Bohr’s Equation: Bohr’s equation is used to measure physiological dead space (which includes both anatomical and alveolar dead space) rather than just anatomical dead space.

 

Option C. Spirometer: A spirometer measures lung volumes and capacities, but it cannot distinguish anatomical dead space from alveolar ventilation.

 

Option D. 133Xe Inhalation: 133Xe (Xenon) is a radioactive gas used in ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scanning to assess regional lung ventilation but is not a standard method for measuring anatomical dead space.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Anatomical dead space is best measured using the Single Breath Nitrogen Test (Fowler’s Method), which evaluates the washout of nitrogen during a controlled exhalation.

questions.stemHtml: The following is a recording of static pressure volume curve of lungs, from different patients. What does the “B” curve represent?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Interstitial fibrosis

 

The static pressure-volume curve shows the relationship between lung volume and transpulmonary pressure during passive inflation and deflation of the lungs. The compliance (ease of expansion) of the lung determines the shape of this curve.

 

  • Curve A (Above Normal): Represents Emphysema. In emphysema, lung compliance is increased due to loss of elastic fibers, making the lungs more distensible. Less pressure is needed to expand the lungs, leading to a curve that is shifted upward and leftward.
  • Curve B (Below Normal): Represents Interstitial Fibrosis. In fibrosis, lung compliance is decreased due to excessive fibrotic tissue, making the lungs stiff and harder to expand. This results in a curve that is shifted downward and rightward, requiring higher pressures to inflate the lungs.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Emphysema: Emphysema is associated with higher lung compliance, which is represented by Curve A (uppermost curve).

 

Option B. Normal: The normal curve is already labeled in the middle, making this option invalid for Curve B.

 

Option D. Asthma: Asthma is primarily an obstructive lung disease, affecting airflow resistance rather than lung compliance. It does not cause a restrictive pattern, making it an incorrect answer.

 

Educational Objective:

 

A downward-shifted pressure-volume curve indicates decreased lung compliance, characteristic of restrictive lung diseases like interstitial fibrosis. In contrast, emphysema increases lung compliance, shifting the curve upward.

questions.stem: Na-I transporter is present in all except?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Pituitary 

 

The sodium-iodide symporter (NIS) is a membrane protein that plays a crucial role in iodide uptake from the bloodstream into certain tissues. It is essential for thyroid hormone synthesis and is also expressed in other iodide-concentrating tissues.

 

  • Present in:
    • Thyroid gland (for thyroid hormone production)
    • Salivary glands (minor role in iodide secretion)
    • Placenta (for fetal iodide supply)
    • Mammary glands (during lactation for iodine transfer into breast milk)
    • Gastrointestinal tract
  • Absent in:
    • Pituitary gland does not express the sodium-iodide transporter (NIS) because it does not require iodide for its function. The pituitary regulates thyroid activity via TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) but does not concentrate iodide itself.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Salivary: The salivary glands express NIS, but the iodide absorbed here is not used for hormone production. It is excreted into saliva and reabsorbed in the GI tract.

 

Option C. Placenta: The placenta expresses NIS to transport iodine from the maternal circulation to the fetus, which is essential for fetal thyroid hormone production.

 

Option D. Thyroid: The thyroid gland has the highest expression of NIS, allowing it to concentrate iodide for the synthesis of T3 and T4 hormones.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The sodium-iodide symporter (NIS) is responsible for iodide uptake in the thyroid, salivary glands, placenta, and mammary glands but is absent in the pituitary gland.

questions.stem: Feed forward control system is employed during the regulation of:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Temperature

 

A feed-forward control system is a predictive mechanism that anticipates changes and responds before a disturbance occurs, rather than reacting to changes after they happen (which is the role of feedback control).

 

  • Temperature regulation involves a feed-forward mechanism, especially during conditions like exercise or exposure to a hot or cold environment.
  • The hypothalamus receives signals from skin thermoreceptors and initiates a response before core body temperature changes, thereby minimizing fluctuations.

 

For example:

 

  • When entering a hot environment, sweat production begins before there is a significant increase in body temperature.
  • When exposed to cold, shivering or vasoconstriction is activated before core temperature drops too low.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Blood volume: Blood volume regulation follows a negative feedback mechanism, involving hormones like ADH (vasopressin), renin-angiotensin system (RAAS), and aldosterone.

 

Option B. pH: pH homeostasis is maintained by buffer systems (bicarbonate, phosphate, protein buffers) and respiratory/kidney regulation, all of which are based on negative feedback.

 

Option D. Blood pressure: Blood pressure is regulated via baroreceptors and chemoreceptors, which use feedback mechanisms (negative feedback) rather than feed-forward control.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Feed-forward control is used in temperature regulation, where the body anticipates changes and initiates responses before a significant deviation in core temperature occurs. Other physiological parameters like blood volume, pH, and blood pressure rely on feedback mechanisms.

questions.stem: Maximum area in homunculus signifies which one of the following?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Increased preciseness of movements

 

The sensory and motor homunculus is a representation of the human body mapped onto the primary motor and sensory cortices of the brain. The size of each body part in the homunculus is proportional to the level of motor control or sensory perception, rather than physical size.

 

  • Areas with fine, precise movements (like the fingers, lips, and tongue) occupy the largest area in the motor cortex.
  • This is because these regions require greater neural control for executing precise, skillful, and voluntary movements.
  • Conversely, areas with gross, less refined movements (like the trunk or thighs) take up smaller areas in the homunculus.

 

Thus, a larger area in the homunculus signifies more precise, finely controlled movements, not the number of muscle fibers.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Low control and skilled movements: If a region has a large representation, it indicates high control and precision, not low control.

 

Option B. More muscle fibers are present: The number of muscle fibers does not determine cortical representation. Instead, it depends on how fine the movement control needs to be. For example, the fingers and lips have high representation but do not have more muscle fibers than the legs.

 

Option D. None of the above: Since precision and skillful movements are associated with larger cortical areas, option C is correct.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The areas with maximum representation in the motor homunculus correspond to parts of the body that require precise, fine motor control, such as the hands, lips, and tongue. The size of the representation depends on the degree of motor control, not the number of muscle fibers.

questions.stem: A patient diagnosed with neurodegenerative disease experiences muscle weakness and difficulty walking. The condition is linked to impaired axonal transport, leading to neuronal dysfunction. Considering the patient's symptoms and the critical role of cellular components, which function is not primarily associated with microtubules?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) None of the above 

 

Microtubules are critical components of the cytoskeleton and are composed of tubulin proteins. They serve multiple essential functions in the cell, neurons, and mitotic division. Since all the listed functions involve microtubules, none of them are unrelated to microtubule function.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Spindle Formation: Associated with Microtubules

 

  • During cell division (mitosis & meiosis), microtubules form the mitotic spindle, which helps separate chromosomes into daughter cells.

 

Option B. Cargo Transport: Associated with Microtubules

 

  • Microtubules act as tracks for intracellular transport, helping motor proteins like dynein and kinesin transport vesicles, organelles, and other cellular cargo along axons and dendrites.
  • Impaired axonal transport is a key feature of neurodegenerative diseases like ALS (Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis), Alzheimer’s, and Parkinson’s Disease.

 

Option C. Mitosis (C): Associated with Microtubules

 

  • Microtubules play a direct role in mitosis, ensuring proper chromosome alignment and segregation.

 

Since all three functions are directly associated with microtubules, the correct answer is D) None of the above.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Microtubules are essential for spindle formation, intracellular cargo transport, and mitosis. Their dysfunction is associated with neurodegenerative diseases, where impaired axonal transport leads to neuronal degeneration.

questions.stem: The intrapleural pressure will be A 40-year-old healthy male participates in a study at a respiratory physiology lab. The researchers are measuring various respiratory parameters, including intrapleural pressure, to better understand the mechanics of breathing. One of the researchers asks the students to identify the normal intrapleural pressure at the base of the lungs during the start of inspiration in a healthy adult. What would be the answer?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) – 2.5 mm Hg 

 

The intrapleural pressure (IPP) is the pressure within the pleural cavity, which is always negative due to the opposing forces of the lung’s elastic recoil (inward pull) and the chest wall expansion (outward pull). This negative pressure prevents lung collapse and aids in normal breathing mechanics.

 

  • At the start of inspiration, the diaphragm contracts, increasing the thoracic volume and further reducing the intrapleural pressure.
  • At the base of the lung, where the lung is more compressed due to gravity, the normal intrapleural pressure at the start of inspiration is approximately –2.5 mm Hg.

 

Educational Objective:

 

At the start of inspiration, the intrapleural pressure at the base of the lung is approximately –2.5 mm Hg. This negative pressure helps maintain lung expansion and facilitates airflow into the lungs during inspiration.

questions.stem: During a medical simulation exercise, a patient presents with respiratory distress. The medical team is discussing the various pressures involved in the respiratory system. Which of the following statements accurately describes the relationship between the different pressures in the pulmonary circulation for this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Intrapleural pressure is always greater than intrapulmonary pressure (IPP) during inspiration.

options.label: B
options.text: Transpulmonary pressure (TPP) is the difference between intrapleural pressure (ITP) and Intrapulmonary pressure.

options.label: C
options.text: Intrapulmonary pressure (IPP) is always higher than atmospheric pressure.

options.label: D
options.text: Trans-respiratory pressure is the difference between intrapleural pressure (ITP) and transpulmonary pressure (TPP).

questions.answerText: Transpulmonary pressure (TPP) is the difference between intrapleural pressure (ITP) and Intrapulmonary pressure.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Transpulmonary pressure (TPP) is the difference between intrapleural pressure (ITP) and Intrapulmonary pressure.

 

Understanding pressure relationships in the respiratory system is crucial for managing respiratory distress. The key pressures involved include:

 

  1. Intrapleural Pressure (ITP): The pressure within the pleural cavity, which is always negative under normal conditions to prevent lung collapse.
  2. Intrapulmonary (Alveolar) Pressure (IPP): The pressure inside the alveoli, which fluctuates with breathing and can be positive or negative relative to atmospheric pressure.
  3. Transpulmonary Pressure (TPP): The pressure difference between intrapulmonary (alveolar) pressure and intrapleural pressure. It maintains lung inflation and prevents alveolar collapse. TPP=IPP−ITP

 

Thus, Option B is correct because transpulmonary pressure (TPP) is calculated as the difference between intrapleural pressure (ITP) and intrapulmonary (alveolar) pressure (IPP).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Intrapleural pressure is always greater than intrapulmonary pressure (IPP) during inspiration: False. Intrapleural pressure is always lower (more negative) than intrapulmonary (alveolar) pressure during both inspiration and expiration. This negative pressure helps keep the lungs inflated.

 

Option C. Intrapulmonary pressure (IPP) is always higher than atmospheric pressure: False. 

 

  • Intrapulmonary pressure fluctuates during respiration:
    • During inspiration, IPP is lower than atmospheric pressure, allowing air to flow in.
    • During expiration, IPP is higher than atmospheric pressure, pushing air out.

 

Option D. Trans-respiratory pressure is the difference between intrapleural pressure (ITP) and transpulmonary pressure (TPP): False. Trans-respiratory pressure is actually the difference between intra-alveolar (IPP) and atmospheric pressure, not between ITP and TPP.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Transpulmonary pressure (TPP) is the key pressure maintaining lung inflation and is calculated as the difference between intrapulmonary (alveolar) pressure and intrapleural pressure. Intrapleural pressure is always negative and lower than intrapulmonary pressure during the respiratory cycle.

questions.stem: During a medical physiology lecture, the professor discusses the concept of A-V (arterial-venous) oxygen difference and its variations in different types of hypoxia. The students are asked to identify the type of hypoxia in which the least A-V oxygen difference is observed.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Histotoxic hypoxia.

 

The arterial-venous (A-V) oxygen difference represents the amount of oxygen extracted by tissues from the blood. Different types of hypoxia impact this difference based on oxygen availability and tissue utilization.

 

  • Histotoxic hypoxia occurs when tissues are unable to utilize oxygen despite its availability in the bloodstream.
  • This is often caused by cyanide poisoning, which inhibits cytochrome oxidase (Complex IV) in the electron transport chain.
  • Since the tissues cannot extract oxygen, venous oxygen content remains high, leading to a decreased A-V oxygen difference.

 

Thus, in histotoxic hypoxia, the A-V oxygen difference is the least because oxygen is not being used effectively by the cells.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hypoxic Hypoxia:

 

  • Hypoxic hypoxia occurs due to low arterial oxygen levels (PaO₂), commonly seen in high altitude, lung diseases, or respiratory failure.
  • Tissues still extract oxygen, so the A-V oxygen difference remains normal or slightly increased.

 

Option B. Anemic Hypoxia: 

 

  • Anemic hypoxia occurs when there is low hemoglobin (Hb) content, reducing the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood.
  • Oxygen delivery is reduced, but the oxygen extraction by tissues remains normal, maintaining a normal A-V oxygen difference.

 

Option C. Stagnant (Circulatory) Hypoxia:

 

  • Stagnant hypoxia occurs when blood flow is reduced, commonly due to shock, heart failure, or ischemia.
  • Due to reduced perfusion, tissues extract more oxygen from the limited blood flow, leading to an increased A-V oxygen difference.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Histotoxic hypoxia shows the least A-V oxygen difference because tissues fail to utilize oxygen efficiently, leading to high venous oxygen levels. In contrast, stagnant hypoxia increases A-V oxygen difference due to reduced blood flow and increased oxygen extraction by tissues.

questions.stem: In a respiratory physiology seminar, the instructor discusses the mechanisms that prevent hyperinflation of the lungs during the breathing cycle. The students are asked to identify the specific reflex that plays a role in preventing lung hyperinflation:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Hering Breuer reflex.

 

The Hering-Breuer reflex is a protective pulmonary reflex that prevents excessive lung inflation.

 

  • It is triggered by stretch receptors (slowly adapting pulmonary stretch receptors) located in the bronchi and bronchioles.
  • When the lungs overinflate, these receptors send inhibitory signals via the vagus nerve (CN X) to the medulla, which inhibits inspiration and stimulates expiration.
  • This prevents overdistension of the lungs and helps regulate tidal volume and respiratory rhythm.

 

This reflex is strong in infants (to regulate breathing), but in adults, it primarily functions during forced or deep breathing.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Irritation Reflex: The irritation reflex is triggered by irritants like smoke, dust, or chemical fumes. It causes reflex coughing or sneezing, but does not regulate lung inflation.

 

Option C. Cushing Reflex: The Cushing reflex is related to increased intracranial pressure (ICP) and is characterized by hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular breathing. It has no role in lung inflation.

 

Option D. Bainbridge Reflex:  The Bainbridge reflex is a cardiovascular reflex triggered by increased venous return. It increases heart rate (tachycardia) to prevent blood pooling in the veins. It is not involved in lung inflation control.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Hering-Breuer reflex prevents excessive lung inflation by activating pulmonary stretch receptors that inhibit further inspiration, ensuring controlled tidal volume and respiratory rhythm.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old patient presents with sensory disturbances in the lower limbs and is being evaluated for potential neurological involvement. The physician suspects a lesion affecting the posterior column of the spinal cord. In the context of this patient's symptoms, which of the following complaint is likely to be incorrect?

options.label: A
options.text: The patient reports a complete loss of vibration sensation in the lower limbs.

options.label: B
options.text: The patient complains of an inability to perceive pressure sensations on the feet.

options.label: C
options.text: The patient describes altered temperature perception in the lower limbs.

options.label: D
options.text: The patient experiences difficulty in sensing joint positions and movements (proprioception) in the legs.

questions.answerText: The patient describes altered temperature perception in the lower limbs.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) The patient describes altered temperature perception in the lower limbs.

 

The posterior column (dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway, DCML) is responsible for fine touch, vibration, proprioception (joint position sense), and pressure sensation. A lesion in this pathway leads to loss of these specific sensations in the affected area.

 

The incorrect statement is Option C (altered temperature perception) because temperature and pain sensations are transmitted by the lateral spinothalamic tract, not the posterior column. A lesion in the posterior column would not affect temperature perception.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. The patient reports a complete loss of vibration sensation in the lower limbs: (Possible Symptom)

 

  • The posterior column carries vibration sensation through Pacinian corpuscles and relays the information to the brain.
  • A lesion in this pathway would result in a loss of vibration sense in the affected limbs.

 

Option B. The patient complains of an inability to perceive pressure sensations on the feet: (Possible Symptom)

 

  • Pressure sensation is carried by the posterior column. Damage to this pathway could lead to reduced perception of pressure in the lower limbs.

 

Option D. The patient experiences difficulty in sensing joint positions and movements (proprioception) in the legs: (Possible Symptom)

 

  • Proprioception (joint position sense) is mediated by the posterior column.
  • Damage to this pathway can cause sensory ataxia (loss of balance with eyes closed, positive Romberg's sign).

 

Educational Objective:

 

The posterior column of the spinal cord is responsible for proprioception, vibration, pressure, and fine touch sensations. Temperature and pain sensations are carried by the lateral spinothalamic tract. A lesion in the posterior column does not affect temperature perception.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man presents with specific sensory deficits, particularly in the detection of low-frequency vibrations and fine textural variations upon tactile examination. To elucidate the underlying pathology of his sensory impairment, the attending neurologist must determine which cutaneous receptors, known for their specialization in tactile sensation, are likely compromised:

options.label: A
options.text: Merkel cells, responsible for the perception of sustained pressure and temperature.

options.label: B
options.text: Meissner corpuscles, specialized for detecting light touch and low-frequency vibrations.

options.label: C
options.text: Pacinian corpuscles, slowly adapting for sensing low-frequency vibrations.

options.label: D
options.text: Ruffini end bulbs, involved in the detection of two point discrimination.

questions.answerText: Meissner corpuscles, specialized for detecting light touch and low-frequency vibrations.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Meissner corpuscles, specialized for detecting light touch and low-frequency vibrations.

 

The cutaneous mechanoreceptors in the skin play distinct roles in tactile sensation. Since the patient has difficulty detecting low-frequency vibrations and fine textures, the most likely affected receptors are the Meissner corpuscles.

 

  • Meissner corpuscles are rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors located in the dermal papillae, especially in the fingertips, palms, and soles.
  • They are specialized for detecting light touch, fine textural changes, and low-frequency vibrations (10-50 Hz).
  • Their dysfunction can lead to reduced sensitivity to fine textures and vibrations, explaining the patient’s sensory impairment.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Merkel cells, responsible for the perception of sustained pressure and temperature:

 

  • Merkel cells are responsible for sustained pressure and fine touch, not low-frequency vibrations.
  • They are slowly adapting receptors, providing information about static touch and shape detection.
  • However, they are not responsible for detecting low-frequency vibrations, making this option incorrect.

 

Option C. Pacinian corpuscles, slowly adapting for sensing low-frequency vibrations:

 

  • Pacinian corpuscles detect high-frequency vibrations (250-300 Hz) rather than low-frequency vibrations.
  • They are rapidly adapting receptors but are more involved in deep pressure and fast vibrations, making them unlikely to be affected in this case.

 

Option D. Ruffini end bulbs, involved in the detection of two point discrimination:

 

  • Ruffini corpuscles detect skin stretch and joint movement, not two-point discrimination or low-frequency vibrations.
  • They are slowly adapting and help in proprioception but do not contribute significantly to tactile texture detection.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Meissner corpuscles are responsible for detecting light touch and low-frequency vibrations. Damage to these receptors leads to impaired fine texture discrimination and reduced sensitivity to low-frequency vibrations. Pacinian corpuscles detect high-frequency vibrations, while Merkel cells and Ruffini endings have different tactile functions.
